title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: Know your trait before you run anything
text:
Know your trait before you run anything
Genetic architecture = the landscape of genetic contributions: how many variants, how large their effects, how frequent they are, and how they interact [Timpson 2017].









Architecture
Variants
Example
Tools




Monogenic
one
phenylketonuria, CF (CFTR)
family, WES/WGS


Oligogenic
few
some lipid traits
targeted seq


Polygenic
many, small
height, T2D
large GWAS


Omnigenic
~all expressed genes
most complex traits
huge GWAS + networks




The omnigenic model: regulatory networks are so interconnected that nearly every expressed gene exerts a tiny “peripheral” effect, funnelled through fewer “core” genes — this is why PRS (W3) works.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Allele frequency × effect size
Common variants tend to have small effects; large-effect variants tend to be rare (purifying selection removes common, large-effect, deleterious variants) [Timpson 2017].
 effect │ rare, large effect
  size  │  •           (Mendelian-like)
        │     • •
        │        • • •
        │             • • • • •   common, small effect
        │                       • • • • •  (typical GWAS hits)
        └──────────────────────────────────── MAF


Sample size is destiny — schizophrenia: ~0 hits at n≈hundreds, 113 loci at n in tens of thousands
Effect size ≠ druggability — common HMGCR SNP explains ~0.26% of LDL variance, yet statins are transformative








Important



Architecture can’t be predicted from heritability alone. Choose your study design after you understand the likely architecture.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Population stratification


If cases & controls differ in ancestry, any ancestry-associated variant looks like a disease hit.
▶️ Fix: PCA on genotypes → include top PCs as covariates so ancestry is absorbed by the model.

glm(disease ~ SNP +
      PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5 +  # ancestry
      age + sex + batch,             # nuisance
    family = binomial)








ImportantAlways report ancestry — and its trade-off



Mixing populations uncorrected → false positives. Restricting to one ancestry → cleaner stats but limited generalizability (see Diversity).

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
The Manhattan plot

library(qqman)

manhattan(gwas_results,
          chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",
          col = c("#185FA5", "#1D9E75"),
          suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5),   # dashed
          genomewideline = -log10(5e-8),   # solid
          highlight = lead_snps,
          main = "GWAS — Type 2 Diabetes (n = 150,000)")

Each point = a variant; x = position, y = −log₁₀(p). “Skyscrapers” are associated loci.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Why the threshold is 5×10⁻⁸


~1 million independent common-variant tests after LD pruning
Bonferroni: 0.05 / 1,000,000 = 5×10⁻⁸ → genome-wide significant
p < 1×10⁻⁵ → conventional suggestive line








Note



This is calibrated for common SNPs. Rare-variant and structural-variant tests (see Beyond SNPs) need their own thresholds.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
QQ plot & genomic inflation (λ)

qq(gwas_results$P, main = "QQ — observed vs expected −log10(p)")

chisq  <- qchisq(gwas_results$P, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
lambda <- median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
cat("Genomic inflation λ =", round(lambda, 3), "\n")



Well-calibrated: hug the diagonal, lift off at the tail (true signal)
Inflated (λ > 1.05): all above diagonal → uncorrected stratification / relatedness
Deflated (λ < 0.95): over-conservative QC → lost power
At very large n, modest λ can be genuine polygenicity — LD-score regression separates the two

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Variation that arrays miss
For some traits, common-SNP GWAS nears signal saturation — the next frontier is variation arrays capture poorly [Harris 2025].








Variant class
What it is
Clinical relevance




CNV
del/dup, kb–Mb
dosage effects; under-tested


Structural
inversions, translocations
disrupt genes / distal regulation


Tandem repeats
variable repeat counts
expansions → neuro disorders


HLA / MHC
hyper-polymorphic
dominates autoimmune signals

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Two examples worth remembering


UGT2B17 deletion → prostate cancer — alters testosterone metabolism; frequency varies by population → population-specific risk, invisible to SNP-only analysis [Harris 2025]
CYP2D6 copy number → drug dosing — deletions vs duplications shift codeine→morphine conversion (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers). Pharmacogenetics: the variant changes the right dose








NoteDosage sensitivity & “human knockouts”



Sequencing enables base-pair CNV calling at biobank scale. Aggregating loss-of-function variants (gnomAD LOEUF) builds dosage-sensitivity maps flagging genes intolerant to disruption — directly useful for clinical variant interpretation.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: A hit is rarely the cause
text:
A hit is rarely the cause
A GWAS hit is usually a tag in LD with the real driver.
rs1234567  p = 3×10⁻²⁴            ← lead SNP (reported)
   ├── rs1234568  r² = 0.98
   ├── rs1234591  r² = 0.95       ← one (or more) is causal
   └── rs1234612  r² = 0.91
   (inherited together in a haplotype block)
Post-GWAS pipeline: 1) Fine-mapping → 2) Functional annotation → 3) Variant→gene → 4) Causal inference

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 0 — Linkage disequilibrium
LD both enables GWAS (one tag stands in for many) and complicates it (can’t tell tag from cause by p alone).

library(LDlinkR)

ld_matrix <- LDmatrix(
  snps  = c("rs1234567", "rs1234568", "rs1234591"),
  pop   = "CEU",            # 1000 Genomes population
  r2d   = "r2",
  token = "your_token"      # free at ldlink.nci.nih.gov
)

LDproxy(snp = "rs1234567", pop = "CEU", r2d = "r2", token = "your_token")







Warning



The LD reference panel must match your sample’s ancestry — a CEU panel on an East Asian cohort corrupts fine-mapping [Schaid 2018].

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 1 — Fine-mapping
Modern fine-mapping is Bayesian: compute a posterior inclusion probability (PIP) per variant, then a credible set — the smallest set containing the causal variant(s) with (e.g.) 95% probability [Schaid 2018].

library(susieR)

# SuSiE = Sum of Single Effects — allows multiple causal signals
susie_fit <- susie(X = genotype_matrix, y = phenotype_vector, L = 10)

cs  <- susie_get_cs(susie_fit, coverage = 0.95)  # 95% credible set(s)
pip <- susie_get_pip(susie_fit)                  # per-variant PIP







Note



Fine-mapping shrinks ~200 correlated SNPs to a credible set of a handful — if the data allow it.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
What controls fine-mapping resolution
Expected PIP rises with λ = N·R²/(1−R²) and falls as nearby SNPs get more correlated [Schaid 2018]:


Larger N → tighter credible sets (cheapest win)
High LD (ρ→1) → causal variants statistically indistinguishable in one sample
Functional annotation as a prior → modest help (90% set ~17.5 → ~13.5 SNPs for lipids); matters most in weak, high-LD regions









TipRobustness checklist




PIPs spread across many SNPs? → you likely can’t resolve one variant here
LD reference matches the sample? (compare allele frequencies)
Do SuSiE / FINEMAP / PAINTOR agree?
Multi-ancestry: assume shared causal variants, allow different effect sizes

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 2 — Functional annotation



Location
Likely mechanism




Coding (missense/nonsense)
direct protein change


Splice site
altered mRNA / isoform


Promoter / 5′UTR
transcription regulation


Enhancer
distal gene regulation


Intergenic / intronic
unknown — needs eQTL / chromatin









Important



~90% of GWAS hits are non-coding, enriched in regulatory elements and eQTLs — which is exactly why epigenomics (W4–W5) is essential for interpretation.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 3 — Variant → gene: colocalization
An eQTL affects a gene’s expression. Colocalization tests whether the GWAS and eQTL signals share the same causal variant.

library(coloc)

coloc_result <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = list(pvalues = gwas_pvals, N = 150000, type = "cc", s = 0.3),
  dataset2 = list(pvalues = eqtl_pvals, N = 500,    type = "quant")
)
coloc_result$summary   # PP.H4 = share one causal variant







Tip



PP.H4 > 0.8 → strong evidence the variant acts through that gene → strong effector candidate.








WarningWatch direction of effect (coherence)



A risk allele can down-regulate a gene that looks up-regulated in patients (“incoherence”) — often an impaired protective response. Direction decides agonist vs antagonist [Reay & Cairns 2021].

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 3 (cont.) — which cell type?
Colocalization names a gene; it doesn’t say which cell. Frameworks like sc-linker integrate scRNA-seq with GWAS via stratified LD-score regression (S-LDSC) [Minton 2022]:


Recovered known biology (T cells in eczema; microglia in Alzheimer’s & MS)
Surfaced candidates (GABAergic neurons in depression — current drugs target serotonin)
Separated disease-state programmes (M cells in ulcerative colitis) from healthy-state



A locus needs both a gene (coloc) and a cell type/state (single-cell) before you claim a mechanism.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 4 — Mendelian randomization

Does elevated LDL cause CAD, or just correlate?

Variants = instruments; randomized at conception → mimic a lifelong RCT, immune to lifestyle/SES confounding.
Genetic variants → LDL level → CAD
   (instrument)    (exposure)  (outcome)

library(TwoSampleMR)

exposure_dat <- extract_instruments("ieu-a-300")            # LDL
outcome_dat  <- extract_outcome_data(snps = exposure_dat$SNP,
                                     outcomes = "ieu-a-7")  # CAD
dat    <- harmonise_data(exposure_dat, outcome_dat)
result <- mr(dat)                                            # IVW + sensitivity







Warning



IV assumptions: (1) relevance, (2) independence of confounders, (3) exclusion restriction. #3 is broken by pleiotropy — always run MR-Egger / weighted median [Reay & Cairns 2021].

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: Existing drugs sit on GWAS signals
text:
Existing drugs sit on GWAS signals
Human genetic evidence ~doubles clinical success, so loci are mined for targets [Reay & Cairns 2021].



Trait
Gene
Drug / class




Schizophrenia
DRD2
antipsychotics


Type 2 diabetes
PPARG
thiazolidinediones


Breast cancer
ESR1
tamoxifen


Bone mineral density
RANKL
denosumab


Rheumatoid arthritis
IL6R
tocilizumab


Psoriasis
IL23R
ustekinumab


LDL cholesterol
HMGCR
statins


Atrial fibrillation
SCN5A
class-1a antiarrhythmics









Note



A SNP near a gene doesn’t prove the gene is causal — follow-up required.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Three genetic strategies for repurposing


Locus → target — Open Targets Genetics, Priority index, MAGMA, TWAS (FUSION, S-PrediXcan)
MR for target validation — cis-variants in a druggable gene as instrument (PCSK9, IL6R)
Direction of effect — decides agonist vs antagonist (ties back to coherence)

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
One variant, many phenotypes
GWAS   : one disease  → scan all variants    → "which variants?"
PheWAS : one variant  → scan all phenotypes   → "what else does it do?"
Typically run over electronic health records (ICD/CPT codes as phenotypes) [Denny 2016].


Pleiotropy mapping — repurposing leads and predictable side-effects
EHR-scale — one biobank → thousands of tests at once
Pharmacogenomic PheWAS (“MedWAS”) — variant → drug response / adverse events (free-text extraction is the bottleneck)

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Why diverse cohorts matter
Most GWAS (→ fine-mapping → PRS) are European-ancestry — a scientific and equity problem [Wojcik 2019].


Missed discovery — variants rare/absent in Europeans are invisible; multi-ethnic PAGE found new associations
Better fine-mapping — different LD patterns break haplotype blocks → smaller credible sets
Poor portability — effect sizes & risk scores don’t transfer → biased clinical use widens disparities








ImportantFor Korean cohorts



Use Korean / East-Asian resources (KoGES, Korea Biobank Array “KCHIP”, TOPMed). Check your base GWAS ancestry matches your target before trusting an association, credible set, or PRS.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Dataset: T2D summary statistics
Public T2D GWAS summary stats (e.g. Mahajan et al. 2022, Nat Genet) — one row per variant, no individual genotypes, hence shareable.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(qqman)

gwas <- read_tsv(here("data", "raw", "t2d_gwas_summary.tsv"))
glimpse(gwas)
# CHR, BP, SNP, A1, A2, FREQ, BETA, SE, P, N, INFO

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 1 — QC on summary stats

gwas_clean <- gwas |>
  filter(!is.na(P), P > 0, P <= 1,
         FREQ > 0.01, FREQ < 0.99,   # common variants
         INFO > 0.8) |>              # imputation quality
  mutate(CHR = as.integer(CHR),
         neglogP = -log10(P))

cat("SNPs before QC:", nrow(gwas), "\n")
cat("SNPs after  QC:", nrow(gwas_clean), "\n")

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 2 — QQ plot & λ

chisq  <- qchisq(gwas_clean$P, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
lambda <- median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
cat("Lambda (GC) =", round(lambda, 4), "\n")

qq(gwas_clean$P,
   main = paste0("QQ — T2D GWAS  (λ = ", round(lambda, 3), ")"),
   col  = "#185FA5")

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 3 — Manhattan plot

sig_snps <- gwas_clean |> filter(P < 5e-8) |> arrange(P)
cat("Genome-wide significant variants:", nrow(sig_snps), "\n")

manhattan(gwas_clean,
          chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",
          col = c("#185FA5", "#1D9E75"),
          suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5),
          genomewideline = -log10(5e-8),
          highlight      = head(sig_snps$SNP, 10),
          main           = "T2D GWAS — Manhattan plot")

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 4 — Annotate top hits

library(biomaRt)

mart     <- useMart("ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl")
top_hits <- sig_snps |> slice_min(P, n = 20)

annotations <- getBM(
  attributes = c("chromosome_name", "start_position",
                 "end_position", "external_gene_name"),
  filters    = "chromosomal_region",
  values     = paste0(top_hits$CHR, ":",
                      top_hits$BP - 5e5, ":", top_hits$BP + 5e5),
  mart       = mart
)
head(annotations)

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 5 — Regional (locus-zoom) plot

library(gassocplot)

# TCF7L2 — most replicated T2D locus
tcf7l2 <- gwas_clean |>
  filter(CHR == 10, BP >= 114700000, BP <= 115000000)

stack_assoc_plot(
  markers = tcf7l2[, c("SNP", "CHR", "BP")],
  z       = tcf7l2$neglogP,
  corr    = ld_matrix_tcf7l2,   # from LDlinkR, ancestry-matched
  traits  = "T2D",
  ylab    = "-log10(p)"
)

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Interrogating any locus


Replicated? in an independent cohort?
LD structure? how big is the credible set?
Functional context? coding, regulatory, eQTL?
Which gene & cell type? nearest ≠ causal
Effect size & direction? small; direction guides drug strategy
Druggable? known/tractable target?

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
What GWAS cannot tell you


Causality alone — association ≠ causation (MR helps, with assumptions)
Rare variants — common-SNP GWAS misses MAF < 1% (need WES/WGS)
Non-SNP variation — CNV/SV/repeats need dedicated methods
Mechanism alone — an enhancer hit says “something regulates something”
Transferability — Euro-centric results may not generalize
Gene × environment — static associations miss dynamic biology




GWAS is the beginning of the story, not the end — which is why the rest of the course exists.

text:

   ├─ W6–W7    Metagenomics   → microbiome mediation?

References

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
For person i, sum the GWAS effect size \(\hat\beta_j\) × allele dosage \(G_{ij}\) over all variants j:
\[\text{PRS}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \hat\beta_j \, G_{ij}\]
Person A:
  rs1001  risk allele × 0.03
+ rs2045  risk allele × 0.02
+ rs8821  non-risk    × 0.00
+ ... (thousands–millions more)
─────────────────────────────────
= PRS 1.42  → top 20% of population → ~3× risk

Crucially, variants below genome-wide significance still carry real signal — PRS deliberately includes them [Reay & Cairns 2021].

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
W2’s omnigenic model: thousands of variants each nudge the trait
Single hits capture a sliver of heritability; aggregation captures much more
PRS is the clinical pay-off of polygenicity — one saliva sample → lifetime genetic predisposition








Note



A PRS is a risk indicator, not a diagnosis. It shifts a probability; it does not determine an outcome.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Coronary artery disease — flags high-risk people for earlier statins
Breast cancer — stratifies risk beyond BRCA1/2; guides screening intensity
Type 2 diabetes — PRS + lifestyle → targeted prevention
Atrial fibrillation — predicts incident AF beyond clinical scores
Prostate / colorectal cancer — screening intensity









TipThe clinician’s question



PRS adds information on top of age, BMI, family history, biomarkers. The bar is always: does it change management?

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 1 — C+T (clumping + thresholding)
The simplest, most interpretable approach:
1. Clump  : keep one SNP per LD block (independent signals)
2. Threshold : keep SNPs below a p-value cutoff (e.g. 5e-8, 0.05, ...)
3. Score  : PRS = Σ (effect size × allele dosage)

library(bigsnpr)

obj.bigsnp <- snp_attach(here::here("data", "raw", "target.rds"))
G <- obj.bigsnp$genotypes

ind.keep <- snp_clumping(
  G,
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  S         = abs(sumstats$beta / sumstats$beta_se),  # rank by |Z|
  thr.r2    = 0.1,
  size      = 500
)







Warning



The p-value threshold is arbitrary — C+T discards sub-threshold signal and needs tuning on a validation set.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 2 — LDpred2 (Bayesian, current standard)
Models LD explicitly and reweights all variants (no hard cutoff) under a Bayesian prior [Reay & Cairns 2021].

# 1) Match summary stats to target
sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, obj.bigsnp$map)

# 2) LD reference (genetic positions → correlation matrix)
POS2 <- snp_asGeneticPos(obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
                         obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
                         dir = here::here("data", "raw", "genetic_maps"))
corr <- snp_cor(G, ind.col = sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`,
                infos.pos = POS2, size = 3 / 1000)

# 3) Estimate h2, then LDpred2-auto (no validation set needed)
ldsc <- with(sumstats, snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                                chi2 = (beta / beta_se)^2, sample_size = n_eff))
multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(corr, sumstats, h2_init = ldsc[["h2"]],
                               vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, 30),
                               burn_in = 500, num_iter = 500)

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Choosing a method








Method
Pros
Cons




C+T
fast, interpretable
loses signal, arbitrary threshold


LDpred2
best accuracy, principled, -auto needs no tuning
slower, needs LD reference


PRSice2
easy, great plots
threshold-based


PRS-CS / PRS-CSx
continuous shrinkage; multi-ancestry
needs Python; LD panel




Clinical research: LDpred2 or PRSice2. Multi-ancestry: PRS-CSx. Consider a composite of several methods to reduce single-method assumptions [Kullo 2025].

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Incremental variance (Nagelkerke R²)
Always report PRS performance above a clinical baseline — never PRS alone.

library(tidyverse); library(DescTools)

prs_data <- read_tsv(here::here("results", "prsice_output.best")) |>
  left_join(phenotype, by = "IID")

null_model <- glm(disease ~ age + sex + PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5,
                  data = prs_data, family = binomial)
full_model <- glm(disease ~ PRS + age + sex + PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5,
                  data = prs_data, family = binomial)

r2_prs <- PseudoR2(full_model, "Nagelkerke") -
          PseudoR2(null_model, "Nagelkerke")
cat("Incremental R² from PRS:", round(r2_prs, 4), "\n")

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Discrimination (AUC)

library(pROC)

roc_null <- roc(prs_data$disease, predict(null_model, type = "response"))
roc_full <- roc(prs_data$disease, predict(full_model, type = "response"))

roc.test(roc_null, roc_full)   # does PRS add discrimination?

ggroc(list(Clinical = roc_null, `Clinical + PRS` = roc_full)) +
  labs(title = "Does PRS improve prediction?", color = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()







Note



A statistically significant AUC bump can still be clinically trivial. Pair AUC with reclassification (NRI) and, above all, calibration.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Calibration — the underappreciated metric
Calibration = do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? [Kullo 2025]


Of people told “10% 10-year risk”, do ~10% develop disease?
A PRS well-calibrated in one population can be miscalibrated in another (different baseline risk, covariate distributions)
Fix by recalibration (update baseline hazard / intercept); assess in independent, population-representative cohorts








Important



Good discrimination ≠ good calibration. A model can rank people correctly yet output systematically wrong probabilities.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Quantile plot — the clinical view

prs_data <- prs_data |> mutate(prs_decile = ntile(PRS, 10))

or_by_decile <- prs_data |>
  group_by(prs_decile) |>
  summarise(n_cases = sum(disease == 1),
            n_ctrl  = sum(disease == 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(odds = n_cases / n_ctrl,
         OR   = odds / odds[prs_decile == 5])   # vs middle decile

ggplot(or_by_decile, aes(prs_decile, OR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "PRS decile", y = "OR vs middle decile",
       title = "Disease risk by PRS decile") +
  theme_minimal()

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Same disease, different PRS → different person flagged
text:
Same disease, different PRS → different person flagged


Two PRSs with similar population AUC can disagree on which individual is high-risk [Kullo 2025]
Mitigations: consensus thresholds (high-risk only if top-tier across ≥2 scores) or a composite score
Risk also changes over time (age, comorbidity, exposures) → re-score with up-to-date methods; keep raw genotypes

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Four questions before the clinic (ACCE)
The 2025 review frames PRS readiness with the ACCE framework [Kullo 2025]:


Analytical validity — does the assay/pipeline measure the score accurately & reproducibly?
Clinical validity — does the score actually associate with the disease in the target population?
Clinical utility — does using it improve outcomes?
Ethical, legal, social implications — equity, consent, insurance, communication



Most PRSs clear analytical and clinical validity; the bottleneck is utility and ELSI.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Evidence for clinical utility is still thin
text:
Evidence for clinical utility is still thin
Few completed RCTs [Kullo 2025]:


MI-GENES (CHD) — PRS-integrated risk → lower LDL at 6 mo, fewer events at 10 yr (earlier/longer statin use)
GenoVA — PRS for 6 diseases (CHD, T2D, AF, breast/colorectal/prostate cancer): effect on time-to-diagnosis
WISDOM / PERSPECTIVE — PRS-guided mammography intensity
eMERGE (US, 10 conditions) and Our Future Health (UK, 5M) — implementation at scale








Note



RCTs are slow and costly — cohort, health-economics, simulation and implementation-science studies all contribute evidence.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Communicating risk: three framings
A percentile alone is not enough — it doesn’t say how much disease risk it explains [Kullo 2025].








Framing
Example
Caveat




Absolute risk
“18% over 10 years”
needs incidence data (often missing)


Relative risk / OR
“2.3× population average”
no baseline anchor


Percentile rank
“top 5% of PRS”
says nothing about absolute magnitude




Absolute risk linked to a guideline action is the most clinically actionable framing.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Integrating PRS into existing risk equations
text:
Integrating PRS into existing risk equations


Breast cancer — BOADICEA: the one clinical equation combining PRS + family history + rare variants + clinical factors
CHD — Pooled Cohort Equations: PRS is ~orthogonal → add log-additively
Most other diseases: no validated absolute-risk equation yet → estimate from epidemiological incidence
Lifetime risk can vary dramatically by PRS centile — e.g. ER-positive breast cancer ~2% to ~31% bottom vs top centile

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
The human barriers


Patients hold deterministic views of genetics; risk is actually probabilistic and modifiable (MI-GENES framed it as mutable)
Run many PRSs at once → most people flagged high-risk for something → alarm fatigue
Primary-care providers often lack genomics training → need CDS tools, a trained “champion user”, and PRS in medical curricula

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Why the EHR changes the game
text:
Why the EHR changes the game
Biobanks now link genotypes to EHRs at population scale, so PRS can be built and applied without a bespoke study [Li 2020].


Khera et al. 2018: a PRS can flag people with risk equivalent to a monogenic mutation (CAD, AF, T2D, IBD, breast cancer)
Rich phenotypes: diagnoses, labs, imaging, meds — plus easy, well-defined controls
Examples: Michigan Genomics Initiative, UK Biobank, National Biobank of Korea, Biobank Japan, China Kadoorie

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Turning an EHR into phenotypes


ICD codes — first-line case/control definitions (but coding practices differ between systems)
NLP on clinical notes — extract phenotypes from free text
PheKB — 50+ portable phenotyping algorithms with high positive predictive value








WarningEHR data is messy




Sparse & irregular — sicker patients have richer records (Geisinger: only 20/143 variables had <25% missingness)
Medication adherence not captured — prescribed ≠ taken
Phenotyping errors propagate into PRS evaluation

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Infrastructure for clinical PRS
A workable pipeline needs more than a model [Kullo 2025]:


PGS Catalog — open repository of published scores (alleles + weights + metadata)
FHIR — standard for moving genomic + clinical data between systems
TRE / cloud — compute PRS on-demand with QC’d pipelines
CDS + EHR dashboard — show PRS alongside family history, smoking, labs
Metadata — record algorithm version + ancestry-specific performance for traceability

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Genetic correlation — how much do two diseases share?
text:
Genetic correlation — how much do two diseases share?
Genetic correlation (r_g) quantifies the overlap in heritable basis between two traits [van Rheenen 2019].


Bivariate LDSC — estimates r_g straight from summary statistics, robust to sample overlap (LD Hub hosts hundreds of traits)
Bivariate GREML — from individual genotypes
e.g. schizophrenia ↔︎ bipolar disorder r_g ≈ 0.6



A high r_g explains comorbidity and shared biology, and predicts cross-disorder risk in relatives — directly relevant when counselling families.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Why clinicians should care about r_g
text:
Why clinicians should care about r_g


Comorbidity — shared genetics anticipates co-occurring diagnoses
Borrowing power — pleiotropy-informed methods (MTAG) boost a small GWAS using a correlated, larger one
Cross-disorder risk — a relative’s risk depends on r_g, kinship, heritability and prevalence








Warning



r_g estimates can be distorted by assortative mating, misclassification, collider bias and stratification — interpret with the same care as MR [van Rheenen 2019].

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: PRS does not transfer across ancestries
text:
PRS does not transfer across ancestries


Most GWAS (→ PRS) are European-ancestry
A European-trained PRS performs ~4–5× worse in African-ancestry individuals [Martin, in Li 2020]
Roots: different allele frequencies, LD, and effect sizes from distinct population history (drift, selection, bottlenecks) [Kullo 2025]
Deploying biased PRS clinically can widen health disparities

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
What to do about it


Prefer ancestry-matched base GWAS; use PRS-CSx / multi-ancestry meta-analysis
Report ancestry-specific performance and recalibrate per population
Invest in diverse cohorts — diversity also sharpens fine-mapping (W2)








ImportantFor Korean patients



Use Korean / East-Asian resources (KoGES, Korea Biobank Array “KCHIP”, National Biobank of Korea, TOPMed). Always check the base GWAS ancestry matches your target before trusting a PRS.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Honest limitations


Not causal — high PRS ≠ will develop disease
Misses rare, high-penetrance variants — BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome need dedicated testing
Misses non-SNP variation — CNV/SV/repeats (W2 §Beyond SNPs)
Gene × environment — genetic risk is modifiable by lifestyle/medication
Not a diagnosis — one input among many, not a verdict
Dynamic — risk and methods both change over time

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Match & compute a C+T PRS

sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, map)

ind  <- sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`
prs_scores <- big_prodVec(G, sumstats$beta, ind.col = ind)

prs_df <- obj.bigsnp$fam |> mutate(PRS = prs_scores)
summary(prs_df$PRS)

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Visualize the distribution

ggplot(prs_df, aes(PRS, fill = factor(affection))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1D9E75", "#D85A30"),
                    labels = c("Control", "Case")) +
  labs(title = "PRS — CAD cases vs controls",
       x = "Polygenic Risk Score", fill = "Status") +
  theme_minimal()

prs_df <- prs_df |>
  mutate(prs_pct  = ntile(PRS, 100),
         top10    = prs_pct >= 90,
         bottom10 = prs_pct <= 10)

table(prs_df$top10, prs_df$affection)   # risk in top 10% vs rest

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
LDpred2-auto (more accurate)

corr <- readRDS(here("data", "processed", "ld_matrix.rds"))  # pre-computed

ldsc <- with(sumstats, snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                                chi2 = (beta / beta_se)^2, sample_size = n_eff))

multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(corr, sumstats, h2_init = ldsc[["h2"]],
                               vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, 30),
                               burn_in = 200, num_iter = 200)

beta_auto   <- sapply(multi_auto, function(a) a$beta_est)
prs_ldpred2 <- big_prodMat(G, beta_auto)

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Key takeaways


PRS turns polygenicity into one actionable number — but it’s a risk indicator, not a diagnosis
Always evaluate incremental value, and don’t forget calibration
Clinical readiness = ACCE, not just AUC; utility evidence is still emerging
The hard parts are portability, communication, and EHR integration — not the maths

title: Bioinformatics for BioMedical Scientists
text:
📑 What is inside each week






NoteW1 · Introduction to Bioinformatics






What Bioinformatics Is 👩‍💻 — the three neighbouring fields; wet lab ➡️ dry lab; the five-stage omics workflow that maps the whole course
Sequencing and Data 🧪 — Sanger, short-read, long-read; FASTQ / BAM / VCF / count matrix; the reference genome and reference bias
Where the Data Lives 🗄️ — GEO, SRA, dbGaP, UK Biobank, GTEx, ENCODE, TCGA, HCA
Statistics You Cannot Avoid 📊 — p-values, multiple testing, batch effects, power
Reproducibility and Study Design ♻️ — the conversation to have before you sequence










NoteW2 · Genomics






Human Genetic Variation 🧬 — SNVs, SVs, repeats; allele frequency and allelic architecture
From Reads to Variants 🔬 — variant calling as inference; WGS vs WES vs array; imputation
Genome-Wide Association Studies 📈 — population structure, the association test, Manhattan and QQ plots, 5×10⁻⁸, linkage disequilibrium
From Association to Function 🔎 — fine-mapping, credible sets, eQTL, colocalization, TWAS
Heritability and Prediction 🧮 — SNP heritability, polygenicity, polygenic risk scores
Genomics in the Clinic 🏥 — cancer genomics, Mendelian randomization, drug target discovery










NoteW3 · Epigenomics






What the Epigenome Is 🎛️ — four layers, four assays; one epigenome per cell type
DNA Methylation 🔵 — bisulfite vs arrays, β and M values, DMPs and DMRs, epigenetic clocks
Histone Modifications and ChIP-seq 🧵 — what the marks mean, input controls, peak calling
Chromatin Accessibility: ATAC-seq 🔓 — the assay, its QC, and footprinting
Reading the Regulatory Genome 📖 — motifs, ChromHMM, ENCODE/Roadmap, Hi-C and TADs
Why This Matters Clinically 🏥 — the bridge from non-coding GWAS hits to mechanism










NoteW4 · Transcriptomics






What RNA-seq Measures 📏 — abundance, not synthesis; and not protein
Experimental Choices ⚙️ — poly(A) vs rRNA depletion, strandedness, replicates, design checklist
From Reads to Counts 🔢 — spliced alignment vs pseudo-alignment; gene vs transcript level
Normalization ⚖️ — library size, gene length, and the composition effect; CPM/TPM/TMM/RLE
Differential Expression 📊 — the negative binomial model, shrinkage, sample size, volcano and MA plots
Making Sense of a Gene List 🧠 — ORA vs GSEA and the three commonest misuses
Beyond Differential Expression 🌐 — WGCNA, deconvolution, splicing, eQTLs










NoteW5 · Single-cell Transcriptomics






Why Single Cell 🔬 — what averaging destroys, and when bulk is still better
Platforms and Sample Choices 🧫 — droplet vs plate vs combinatorial; cells vs nuclei
From Droplets to a Count Matrix 🧮 — barcodes, UMIs, zeros, and QC
Finding Cell Types 🗺️ — HVGs, PCA, UMAP, clustering resolution, annotation
Batch Effects and Integration 🔗 — Harmony/scVI, and over-correction
Statistical Testing 📊 — why per-cell tests are invalid; pseudobulk; differential abundance
Dynamics, Space, and Atlases 🌈 — trajectories, cell–cell communication, spatial, HCA










NoteW6 · Proteomics






Why Measure Proteins 💪 — where the other 80% of protein variance comes from
Mass Spectrometry Basics ⚗️ — the bottom-up workflow, MS2 spectra, DDA vs DIA vs targeted
Identification and Quantification 🏷️ — target–decoy FDR, protein inference, LFQ/TMT/SILAC
The Missing Value Problem 🕳️ — MNAR vs MAR, and why naive imputation is dangerous
Statistical Analysis 📊 — how proteomics differs from RNA-seq statistically
Affinity-Based and Population Proteomics 🩸 — dynamic range, Olink/SomaScan, pQTLs
Frontiers and Pitfalls 🚧 — PTMs, AlphaFold, contamination and pre-analytical variation










NoteW7 · Metagenomics






The Human Microbiome 🦠 — body sites, between-person variation, evidence tiers
Study Design and Sample Handling 🧊 — extraction bias, confounders, the kit-ome
Two Ways to Sequence a Community 🧬 — 16S amplicon vs shotgun; OTUs vs ASVs
Reference Databases and Their Limits 📚 — SILVA, GTDB, microbial dark matter
Diversity 🌿 — alpha, beta, rarefaction, PCoA and PERMANOVA
Statistics for Compositional Data ⚠️ — CLR, and why DA methods disagree
From Association to Causation 🔀 — artifact, confounding, reverse causation, causation
Beyond Bacteria, Beyond DNA 🔭 — virome, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics
🎓 Reading Any Omics Paper Critically — the closing checklist for the whole course

title: Bioinformatics for BioMedical Scientists
text:
⚠️ The traps, by week
If you remember one thing from each chapter, remember these.



Week
The trap




W1
Batch confounded with condition cannot be fixed by any analysis — randomise your sample layout


W2
The lead SNP is usually not causal, and the nearest gene is often the wrong gene


W3
Cell-type composition is the dominant confounder in tissue methylation studies


W4
Bulk differential expression is frequently a composition difference


W5
Per-cell tests are invalid across conditions — your n is the number of donors


W6
You never observe a protein; naive imputation manufactures false positives


W7
Sequencing measures proportions, and DA methods disagree on the same data

title: Bioinformatics for BioMedical Scientists
text:
🧭 How to read each chapter
Every chapter follows the same shape:

🎯 Learning objectives — what you should be able to do afterwards
🤔 Motivating question — the problem the chapter exists to solve
Numbered sections — 1. → 1) → ①, mirroring the lecture
⚠️ Pitfall boxes — the mistakes that show up in real manuscripts
💡 Tips — practical guidance for your own project
📝 Summary · 🔑 Key terms · ➕ References







TipCross-links





Sections marked 🔗 point back to an earlier week. Omics layers are not independent, and the connections are where most of the interesting biology lives — the clearest example runs W2 → W3 → W4 → W6, from a non-coding GWAS hit to a genetically validated drug target.









ImportantWhere this ends up





The course closes with a checklist in W7 §9 for reading any omics paper critically — design, measurement, analysis, interpretation — with pointers back to the chapter that covers each question.
If you can work through that list on a paper in your own field, this course has done its job.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Explain what a bioinformatician does, and what they need from you
Describe the three main sequencing technologies and what each is good for
Say what a FASTQ, BAM, VCF, and count matrix each contain — without opening one
Explain why the choice of reference genome and annotation changes results
Name the major public omics repositories and what lives in each
Recognize the three statistical traps that ruin most omics analyses
Have a productive design conversation before you send samples for sequencing

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
1) Bio + Information
A compound word, and both halves matter.

Bio ➡️ human samples, cells, tissues — with phenotypes attached
Information ➡️ data, usually omics data, usually a very large table




Bioinformatics sits at the intersection of biology, computer science, and statistics — and spans the whole path from sample to interpretation.


The job — turn the second into a statement about the first.
The difficulty — the translation is lossy in both directions:

A tumour ➡️ a matrix of numbers
A matrix of numbers ➡️ a claim about a tumour

Most of this course is about where information leaks out at each step.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
2) Three neighbouring fields
Often used interchangeably. Different jobs.








Field
Central question
Typical output




Bioinformatics
How do I get from raw data to an interpretable measurement?
Processed matrices, variant calls, annotated gene lists


Computational biology
Can I build a model that explains or predicts biology?
Simulations, predictive models, mechanistic theory


Biostatistics
Given this design, what can I legitimately conclude?
Estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, study designs



In practice one person does all three. The distinction matters when deciding who to ask:

“My aligner is throwing away 40% of reads” → bioinformatics
“Is n = 3 enough?” → biostatistics, and it should have been asked months earlier







TipThe most useful thing you will learn this semester





Not how to run anything.
Recognizing which of those three questions you are actually asking — because asking the wrong specialist wastes months.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
3) Wet lab ➡️ dry lab
You already have the right reflexes. A beautiful Western blot prompts: what was the loading control? how many biological replicates? was the exposure saturated?
Same reflexes, different artifacts:







Wet lab habit
Dry lab equivalent




Loading control
Normalization (W4)


Antibody validation
Reference database / annotation choice (W1, W6)


Blinding and randomization
Batch design and randomized sample layout (W1)


Technical vs. biological replicate
The same distinction, more consequential (W4)


“It worked once”
A finding that does not replicate in a second cohort



The failure mode unique to computation — the analysis always produces an answer.

Failed PCR → an empty gel. Obvious
Failed RNA-seq analysis → a tidy table of 847 genes, sorted by p-value. Nothing about its appearance tells you it is wrong

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
4) The generic omics workflow 🗺️
The omics layers of the next six weeks, organized by the central dogma — each with its own characteristic question.



W2 works on the genome, W3 on its regulatory state, W4–W5 on the transcriptome, W6 on the proteome. W7 asks the same questions of a second genome — the microbiome.


Every analysis in this course — genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metagenomics — follows the same five stages.
① Quality control     → is this data usable at all?
② Alignment /          → where did each measurement come from,
   quantification         and how much of it is there?
③ Normalization       → make samples comparable to each other
④ Statistical testing → which differences are larger than noise?
⑤ Interpretation      → what does that mean biologically?






ImportantThis is the map for the whole course





Every week from W2 onward: ask where in these five stages you are. The technologies differ enormously; the stages barely change.
The stages are also where the errors live — and they are not equally dangerous:

Stage ① ② errors → loud. The pipeline crashes, or the numbers are absurd
Stage ③ ④ errors → quiet. These are the ones that reach publication

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
1) Sequencing technologies in one hour
Nearly all omics data here comes from sequencing DNA — even when the question is about RNA, chromatin, or protein binding. The trick that made omics possible: convert every molecular question into “count the DNA fragments.”
The other enabler was economics — cost per genome fell faster than Moore’s law, from ~$100 million in 2001 to a few hundred dollars today.



Cost per human genome. The discontinuity around 2007–2008 is the arrival of massively parallel short-read sequencing. Source: NHGRI.








NoteWhy this graph matters for you






Then — the bottleneck was generating data
Now — the bottleneck is interpreting it, and increasingly, having a design worth interpreting

That shift is the entire reason this course exists.




① Sanger sequencing

chain termination with fluorescently labelled ddNTPs


The original method; still the clinical gold standard for confirming a single variant
One reaction = one template, up to ~800–1,000 bases
Very high per-base accuracy




Sanger sequencing. A ddNTP lacks the 3′-OH needed for the next phosphodiester bond, so incorporation terminates the chain. A ladder of fragments of every length, each labelled by its terminal base, reads out the sequence.


⚠️ The limitation is throughput, not quality. One gene is trivial. One genome took thirteen years and ~$3 billion.


② Short-read sequencing (Illumina)

massively parallel sequencing by synthesis

The key idea — parallelism. Not one molecule read well, but hundreds of millions read simultaneously, each moderately well.
The workflow:

Library preparation — fragment the DNA, ligate adapters to both ends
Cluster generation — each fragment amplified in place on a flow cell
Sequencing by synthesis — one fluorescent, reversibly terminated base per cycle: add, image, unblock; repeat 50–300×




Left: library preparation — fragmentation, adapter ligation, denaturation. Right: bridge amplification on the flow cell, which turns one molecule into a cluster bright enough to image.



The library molecule
Everything entering the sequencer: adapter + insert + adapter. Each component has a job.



P5/P7 bind the flow cell. Rd1/Rd2 SP are the sequencing primer binding sites. Index1/Index2 identify the sample.


Two features matter for interpretation:

Index (barcode) — 6–12 nt, identifies the sample

Enables multiplexing: many samples in one lane, demultiplexed afterwards
⚠️ Also where sample swaps and index hopping happen — reads assigned to the wrong sample. Dual indexing exists because single indexing was not reliable enough

Single-end vs. paired-end — reading the fragment from one end or both




Single-end gives one read per fragment; paired-end gives two, with a known approximate distance between them. That distance is what lets an aligner place reads confidently in repetitive regions and detect splice junctions and rearrangements.



Paired-end costs more → better alignment in repeats, plus structural rearrangements and splice junctions (🔗 W4)
Typical output today: 2 × 150 bp, per-base error ~0.1%
⚠️ Read length is the fundamental limit — 150 bases is shorter than most repeats, most structural variants, and most full-length transcripts




③ Long-read sequencing (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore)

read the whole molecule, accept more errors per base


PacBio HiFi — circular template read repeatedly, consensus taken. ~15–25 kb reads, accuracy comparable to short reads
Oxford Nanopore — single strand threaded through a protein pore, ionic current decoded

Reads can exceed a megabase
Raw accuracy below Illumina, though modern chemistries have narrowed the gap considerably
Detects base modifications (e.g. DNA methylation) directly, without bisulfite conversion (🔗 W3)




④ The trade-off triangle
Read length, per-base accuracy, cost per base — you cannot maximize all three. Every platform picks a corner.











Read length
Accuracy
Cost / Gb
Best for




Sanger
~800 bp
Very high
Very high
Confirming a single variant


Illumina
50–300 bp
High
Low
Counting: RNA-seq, ChIP, WGS/WES at scale


PacBio HiFi
15–25 kb
High
Moderate
Assembly, structural variants, phasing


Nanopore
up to Mb
Moderate
Moderate
Ultra-long spans, direct modification calling, portability









TipThe question to ask about any dataset





Not “which platform?” but “is the read long enough to answer my question?”

Variant in a segmental duplication? → 150 bp reads will not save you
Transcript with ten isoforms differing at the 3′ end? → same

No amount of depth fixes a read-length problem.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
2) The shape of biological data
You will probably never open these files by hand — but you will read methods sections that mention them, and reviewers will ask.
What matters: what each format holds, and what it has already thrown away.

① FASTQ — the raw read
Four lines per read, tens of millions of reads per sample.
@SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51           ← read ID
GCCTTGGTGGTGAAATGGTAGACTGGAATTCTCGGGTGCC   ← sequence
+SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51           ← description
F:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFF   ← base quality (Phred)

Knows — the sequence, and the machine’s confidence in each base
Does not know — where in the genome the read came from. That information does not exist yet


Phred quality score
\[Q = -10 \log_{10} P\]
where \(P\) = probability that the base call is wrong.



Phred score
Error rate
Base call accuracy




10
1 in 10
90%


20
1 in 100
99%


30
1 in 1,000
99.9%


40
1 in 10,000
99.99%



Q30 = the conventional benchmark. “>80% of bases above Q30” is the sort of line you will see in a facility report.



② BAM — reads placed on a genome
Every read + the coordinate the aligner assigned + a mapping quality for that assignment.
⚠️ Alignment is inference, not observation.

A read from a repetitive region could plausibly come from several places
The aligner picks one and lowers the mapping quality to say so
Analyses that ignore mapping quality silently accept a lot of wrong placements

BAM is where read-level information ends for most projects — large (tens of GB per WGS sample), and everything downstream is a summary of it.


③ VCF — differences from a reference
Positions where your sample differs from the reference, with genotype and quality. Everything shared with the reference is implicit and absent.
⚠️ A VCF is a diff, not a genome.

A region that could not be aligned produces no variants
That looks identical to a region with no variants
Absence of a call ≠ a call of absence



④ Count matrix — where most analyses actually begin
Features (genes, peaks, proteins, taxa) in rows × samples in columns, one number per cell.

What public repositories distribute, and what statistical methods consume
Also the point of maximum information loss — every read, alignment, and quality score compressed into one integer per gene per sample







WarningWhat the count matrix has already decided for you





By the time it reaches you, someone has already chosen:

Reference genome build
Annotation version
Aligner
Quantification method
Rules for multi-mapping reads

All invisible in the matrix. All capable of changing your results substantially.
→ Download a matrix from GEO, and the original paper’s methods section is part of your methods section.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
3) The reference genome

① GRCh38 and T2T-CHM13
Not a person’s genome — a mosaic from several donors, curated over two decades. An idealized coordinate system everyone agrees to use.

GRCh38 (2013) — the workhorse. Still the default for most clinical and population resources, largely because enormous datasets are already mapped to it
T2T-CHM13 (2022) — the first genuinely complete assembly: centromeres, acrocentric short arms, and other GRCh38 gaps. Adds ~200 Mb of previously unmapped sequence
Pangenome references — a graph of many haplotypes rather than one linear sequence. Where the field is heading; not yet the default

⚠️ Coordinates are not interchangeable between builds.

A position in GRCh37 (hg19) is a different position in GRCh38
“Liftover” is routine but lossy
Mixing builds is one of the commonest sources of nonsense results in student projects



② Annotation: where the genes are

Reference sequence — what the bases are
Annotation — which stretches are genes, exons, transcripts, regulatory elements

Separate files, separately versioned, and they disagree with each other.

GENCODE — comprehensive; used by ENCODE and GTEx. Includes many lncRNAs and predicted transcripts
RefSeq — NCBI’s conservative, manually curated set. Standard in clinical reporting

~20,000 protein-coding genes — a remarkably stable number. But transcript counts differ by tens of thousands between sources and versions.






WarningAnnotation version is a hidden variable





Same FASTQ files + different GENCODE release →

different gene counts
different library totals
→ different normalization factors
→ different DE results

Usually modest differences. Occasionally not.
Report the build and the annotation version. Every time.





③ Reference bias
Everything is measured relative to one sequence → anything poorly represented in that sequence is systematically under-detected.

Divergent haplotypes — reads from non-European-ancestry individuals map slightly worse to a reference built mostly from European donors → subtle allele-frequency and coverage biases (🔗 W2)
Highly polymorphic loci — HLA is the classic case; standard alignment badly misrepresents it
Repetitive and duplicated regions — reads map ambiguously or not at all
Sequence absent from the reference — undetectable by definition

🗺️ First appearance of a thread running through the whole course: reference bias.

W3 → chromatin atlases
W4 → annotation versions
W6 → the protein search database
W7 → the 16S taxonomy database

Same problem, different name.
