This chapter’s ordering principle: regulatory logic. Accessibility as the gate → what kind of element sits there → which promoter it reaches → and finally the DNA-level layer, which has its own distinct measurement problems.

title: W3. Epigenomics
section: 4) What is and is not heritable
text:
4) What is and is not heritable
“Epigenetic” carries baggage. Two very different claims get conflated:

✅ Mitotic heritability — a methylation pattern copied to daughter cells at division. Well established; the basis of cell identity
⚠️ Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance — a mark acquired by a parent passed to offspring and grandchildren

Real in plants and C. elegans
In mammals: contested, mechanism unclear — the germline undergoes near-complete epigenetic reprogramming twice


💡 When you read “epigenetic inheritance”, check which claim is being made.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
1) The principle
ATAC-seq — a hyperactive Tn5 transposase, preloaded with sequencing adapters.

Tn5 inserts preferentially where DNA is not wrapped in nucleosomes — i.e. where regulatory proteins are actively holding chromatin open
Fragmentation and adapter ligation happen in one step → fast protocol, works from few cells







ImportantAccessibility is a genuine prerequisite — for this assay only






ATAC is performed on intact nuclei. Tn5 must physically reach the DNA in situ
→ closed chromatin is invisible to ATAC by construction

Compare with ChIP (§3.2), where chromatin is fragmented before the antibody ever meets it. This distinction is worth holding onto: it is the reason ATAC and ChIP see different things, and it is often stated backwards.

title: W3. Epigenomics
section: 2) Why it is the natural first assay
text:
2) Why it is the natural first assay

No antibody → no antibody-quality problem, no target chosen in advance
One experiment → a first-pass regulatory map of a cell type, with no prior hypothesis about which factor to pull down
Promoters, active enhancers, and TF-bound sites, all at once

⚠️ What it does not tell you: which kind of element you found. An open region could be a promoter, an enhancer, an insulator, or a repressed-but-primed element. That is §3.

title: W3. Epigenomics
section: 3) QC — the two figures to demand
text:
3) QC — the two figures to demand



Both panels are diagnostic. Neither is optional.



Fragment size distribution

✅ A nucleosome-free peak below ~100 bp, then ~200 bp periodicity from mono-, di-, tri-nucleosomes
❌ A smooth, featureless curve → the transposition failed

TSS enrichment

Promoters are open in essentially every cell type → a sharp peak at TSSs is a floor expectation, not a finding
❌ A flat TSS profile → the assay failed. Not unusual biology

Mitochondrial fraction

mtDNA has no nucleosomes → Tn5 attacks it enthusiastically
Untreated protocols can waste well over half the reads on chrM; Omni-ATAC and similar improvements reduce this

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
4) Footprinting, and its limits

A bound transcription factor protects its own site from Tn5 → a small dip inside a larger accessible region
In principle: locate specific factors without ChIP

⚠️ In practice, unreliable for many factors:

Tn5 has its own sequence insertion bias that mimics footprints
Factors with short residence times leave no protection at all

→ Treat footprint-based factor calls as hypotheses.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
1) What the marks mean
Dozens exist. Five do most of the work in genomics.








Mark
Indicates
Shape of signal




H3K4me3
Active promoter
Sharp, at TSS


H3K27ac
Active promoter or enhancer
Sharp-ish, flanking the element


H3K4me1
Enhancer — primed or active
Broad


H3K27me3
Polycomb-repressed
Broad domains


H3K9me3
Constitutive heterochromatin
Very broad, repeats



The key interpretive move — no single mark identifies an element. Combinations do.

H3K4me3 + H3K27ac → active promoter
H3K4me1 + H3K27ac → active enhancer
H3K4me1 alone → primed enhancer — poised, not firing
H3K4me3 + H3K27me3 → bivalent — developmental genes held ready in stem cells

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
2) ⚠️ ChIP does not require accessibility
A common misconception, worth stating explicitly.
ATAC   nuclei intact → Tn5 must reach the DNA in situ
                     → accessibility IS required

ChIP   crosslink (formaldehyde)
       → shear / MNase-digest the chromatin
       → antibody meets FRAGMENTS in solution
                     → accessibility is NOT required
→ This is exactly why ChIP can map H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 — marks that define the most tightly closed chromatin in the nucleus, which ATAC cannot see at all.
The two assays are complementary, not redundant.

title: W3. Epigenomics
section: 3) The assay, and the control you must have
text:
3) The assay, and the control you must have
Two failure points dominate:

⚠️ Antibody quality — ChIP-seq is an antibody experiment. Specificity for histone modifications is variable and lot-dependent. A wet-lab problem no analysis can repair
⚠️ The input control — chromatin does not fragment uniformly:

open regions shear more easily
copy number varies
→ without a matched input (sonicated chromatin, no antibody) or IgG control, you cannot tell enrichment from artifact

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
4) Peak calling and QC
Peak calling — compare signal to control, identify regions of significant enrichment. MACS2 and successors are standard.

Parameters matter: narrow mode for point-source marks (H3K4me3), broad mode for domains (H3K27me3)

Useful QC numbers:

FRiP (fraction of reads in peaks) — how much sequencing went into signal rather than background. Low FRiP → weak IP
Cross-correlation (NSC / RSC) — whether strand-shifted signal shows the expected structure
Library complexity — distinct fragments vs. PCR duplicates

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
5) CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
The problem with ChIP: many cells needed, lots of background.
The fix — tether the cleaving enzyme (MNase, or Tn5) directly to the antibody → only the targeted region is released or tagged.

Far higher signal-to-noise, from thousands of cells rather than millions
This is what made single-cell chromatin profiling practical (🔗 W5)

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
6) Reading the tracks together



The combination of tracks, not any single one, tells you what kind of element you are looking at.


The single most common figure in the epigenomics literature. Reading it is a concrete skill — work top to bottom, then across:

ATAC peak? → something is open here (§2)
H3K4me3 dominant? → promoter. H3K4me1 dominant? → enhancer
H3K27ac on top? → the element is active in this cell type, not merely present
H3K27me3 domain? → repressed, regardless of what else is there
Compare to input — if the “peak” is also in input, it is not a peak

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
1) The assay
Hi-C — crosslink chromatin → digest → ligate whatever ends are physically close → sequence the junctions.
Output: a matrix of contact frequencies between every pair of genomic bins.



Contact frequency falls with distance, but not smoothly — the blocks are the point.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
2) What the matrix shows

A/B compartments — megabase-scale segregation into active (A) and inactive (B) chromatin
TADs (topologically associating domains) — sub-megabase blocks, frequent internal contacts, sharp CTCF-bound boundaries

Boundaries are largely conserved across cell types

Loops — specific enhancer–promoter contacts

Not conserved across cell types
→ these are what you actually want for variant interpretation

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
3) ⚠️ Contact is not function

A loop says two regions are near each other
It does not say the enhancer regulates that promoter

→ Perturbation experiments (CRISPRi on the element) are what establish function.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
1) Measurement

① Bisulfite sequencing
Sodium bisulfite converts unmethylated C → U (read as T); methylated C is protected and still reads as C. Sequence, compare to reference: a C that stayed C was methylated.

WGBS — every CpG, single-base resolution. Expensive; needs deep coverage because sequence complexity drops after conversion
RRBS — enzymatic digestion enriches CpG-dense regions. Far cheaper, biased subset

⚠️ Two limitations of bisulfite:

It degrades DNA
It cannot distinguish 5mC from 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) — abundant in brain, different biology

Alternatives: EM-seq (enzymatic conversion, no degradation); long-read platforms call modifications directly from raw signal, with no conversion at all (🔗 W1 §2.1③).


② Arrays
Illumina EPIC — a fixed panel of CpG sites, on the order of 850,000 for v1 (~3% of all CpGs), enriched for promoters, enhancers, and known disease loci.
Same trade-off as genotyping arrays (🔗 W2 §2.3):

❌ Cannot discover anything outside the panel
✅ Cheap enough to run on thousands of samples → almost all large epidemiological methylation studies use them

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
2) β values and M values



Left: real methylation data is bimodal. Right: the transformation almost every analysis applies before testing.



β value — the intuitive quantity: proportion of DNA molecules methylated at a site, 0 to 1

\[
\beta = \frac{M}{M + U + \alpha}
\]

M value — its logit transform, \(\log_2(\beta / (1-\beta))\)

Why bother:

β is bounded at 0 and 1 → variance compressed at both extremes → exactly where most CpGs sit
→ violates linear model assumptions
M is unbounded and roughly homoscedastic

💡 The convention — test on M values, report and plot β values.
⚠️ A paper running t-tests directly on β at CpGs with β ≈ 0.02 is doing something statistically dubious.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
3) Differential methylation

① DMP vs. DMR

DMP (differentially methylated position) — a single CpG differing between groups
DMR (differentially methylated region) — a run of adjacent CpGs changing together

DMRs are more believable — neighbouring CpGs are biologically correlated, so a consistent regional shift is harder to produce by chance or by one bad probe.
⚠️ A lone significant CpG in an otherwise flat region deserves suspicion.


② ⚠️ Cell-type composition
The most important subsection in the chapter.



The mechanism of the field’s most common false positive.








WarningCell composition is the dominant confounder





The mechanism:

Methylation differs enormously between cell types — far more than between individuals or disease states within one cell type
→ cases and controls with even slightly different cell mixtures
→ thousands of CpGs appear “differentially methylated”
→ without a single cell having changed anything

Not hypothetical. Disease, infection, medication, age, and smoking all shift blood cell proportions.
→ A blood methylation study that does not adjust for cell composition is, to a first approximation, a study of cell counts.
What to do:

✅ Measure cell counts directly if possible (CBC, flow cytometry) → include as covariates
✅ Otherwise reference-based deconvolution (Houseman method and successors) → estimate proportions from the methylation data itself, then adjust
✅ Reference-free methods (RefFreeEWAS, ReFACTor, SVA) for tissues without reference panels — at the cost of possibly removing real signal too
✅ State exactly what you did. “We adjusted for cell composition” with no detail is not enough

🔗 The chapter-spanning version of W1 §4.3’s confounding thread. It returns in W4 §7.2 as bulk tissue deconvolution, and in W5 §6.3 as differential abundance.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
4) Epigenetic clocks ⏳
Take a few hundred CpGs whose methylation changes with age → fit a penalised regression against chronological age → a predictor accurate to within a few years.



The prediction is not the interesting part. The residual is.


Age acceleration — the residual. How much older or younger someone looks epigenetically than their birth certificate says.

Associated with mortality, cardiovascular disease, and a long list of exposures







WarningThree things to check before believing a clock result





① Which clock?

1st generation (Horvath, Hannum) — trained to predict chronological age → by construction, penalised for detecting biological ageing
2nd generation (PhenoAge, GrimAge) — trained against clinical biomarkers and mortality → predict health outcomes considerably better
→ not interchangeable; results do not transfer between them

② Cell composition again. Blood clock signals are partly driven by immune cell proportions shifting with age. Adjusted or not?
③ Association, not mechanism. Age acceleration is a biomarker. Nothing about a clock says whether methylation causes ageing or merely records it.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
1) Transcription factor motif analysis
Given a set of peaks: which TF binding motifs are over-represented relative to a background set? Tools: HOMER, MEME suite, chromVAR (single-cell).
⚠️ Two chronic problems:

Background choice determines the answer. GC-matched, accessibility-matched background is essential. Random genomic regions inflate everything
Motif similarity. Family members are indistinguishable — “the AP-1 motif” does not tell you FOS vs. JUN vs. a dozen relatives

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
2) Chromatin states and reference atlases
ChromHMM — learns recurring combinations of marks, labels every genomic segment with a state (“active TSS”, “weak enhancer”, “heterochromatin”). Converts five noisy tracks into one interpretable annotation.



Resource
What it holds




ENCODE
Uniformly processed ChIP, ATAC, RNA across hundreds of cell types; candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs)


Roadmap Epigenomics
Chromatin states across 127 primary tissues and cell types


UCSC / WashU browsers
Where you look at all of the above over your locus



🗺️ These atlases are also a reference bias problem (🔗 W1 §2.3③):

Your cell type not in ENCODE? → the annotations you inherit come from something else
→ elements active only in your cells are invisible

title: W3. Epigenomics
section: 3) From a non-coding GWAS hit to a mechanism
text:
3) From a non-coding GWAS hit to a mechanism
Recall: ~90% of GWAS associations are non-coding (🔗 W2 §4.3). A variant in intergenic space is uninterpretable alone. Epigenomics supplies the missing annotation.
① GWAS signal, fine-mapped to a credible set        (W2 §4.2)
② Overlap credible-set variants with ATAC / H3K27ac
   peaks — in the disease-relevant cell type         (§2, §3)
③ Which TF motif does the risk allele disrupt?       (§6.1)
④ Which promoter does that enhancer contact?         (§4)
⑤ Does the target gene's expression change?          (eQTL, W4)
⑥ Does deleting or editing the element do anything?  (CRISPR)
Partitioned heritability (LDSC-SEG, stratified LD score regression) runs the same logic in aggregate rather than locus by locus:

Which cell types’ regulatory annotations are enriched for a trait’s heritability?
→ often the strongest available evidence about which tissue a disease lives in — microglia for Alzheimer disease, specific T cell subsets for autoimmune disease

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
4) ⚠️ The central problem: which cells?






WarningThe right annotation in the wrong cell type is worthless






An enhancer active in hepatocytes → invisible in a lymphoblastoid cell line
Overlap your credible set with the wrong cell type’s peaks → you find nothing
→ “no overlap” is indistinguishable from “wrong reference”

This is why the field pushed so hard toward single-cell chromatin profiling (🔗 W5), and why choosing which ENCODE cell types to use is a scientific decision, not a technical default.

title: W3. Epigenomics
text:
5) Where epigenetics is already clinical

Methylation-based tumour classification — CNS tumour classifiers on methylation arrays now outperform histopathology for some entities; in routine diagnostic use
Cell-free DNA — plasma DNA methylation carries a tissue-of-origin signal → the basis of multi-cancer early detection assays
Epigenetic drugs — DNMT inhibitors (azacitidine, decitabine) and HDAC inhibitors approved in haematological malignancy; EZH2 inhibitors in specific lymphomas and sarcoma
Imprinting disorders — Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes diagnosed by methylation testing

title: W2. Genomics
text:
1) Types of variation
A typical human genome, compared to the reference (🔗 W1 §2.3):

~4–5 million single nucleotide variants and short indels
~20,000–25,000 structural variants

⚠️ The second number is far smaller — but SVs collectively affect more base pairs than all SNVs combined. Count and impact point in opposite directions, and this decides which technology you need.



Classes of variation, drawn against the same reference sequence. The boundary between “indel” and “structural variant” is a convention — conventionally 50 bp — not a biological distinction.



① SNVs and short indels

SNV — one base changed
Indel — a short insertion or deletion
What most people mean by “a variant”, and what arrays, exomes, and standard short-read pipelines detect well

💡 Terminology: SNP (polymorphism) is used for common variants, SNV for any single-base change including somatic and rare ones. Usage is not consistent across the literature.


② Structural variants and copy number
Anything larger than ~50 bp — deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions, translocations. CNVs = the subset that changes dosage.
⚠️ Short reads detect SVs poorly.

A 150 bp read cannot span a 10 kb deletion
→ SV calling from short reads is inference from indirect signals: abnormal read-pair distances, coverage drops, split reads
→ high false positive rates
→ the single strongest argument for long reads (🔗 W1 §2.1③)



③ Tandem repeats

Short sequences repeated head-to-tail, varying in copy number between individuals
Expansions cause Huntington disease, fragile X, and a growing list of neurological disorders
⚠️ Almost invisible to standard short-read pipelines; their contribution to common disease is only now being assessed systematically







WarningEvery technology has a blind spot





“No significant variants in gene X” honestly means: no variants of the classes this assay can detect.
A negative exome result says nothing about:

intronic variants
structural variants
repeat expansions

title: W2. Genomics
text:
2) Allele frequency: common vs. rare
Allele frequency — the proportion of chromosomes in a population carrying a given allele.

Common — minor allele frequency (MAF) above 1–5%
Rare — below

This one number determines almost everything about study design, because frequency and effect size are inversely related — and not by accident:

Strong deleterious effects → removed by selection
→ a variant both common and highly damaging would already have been eliminated, or found decades ago




Allelic architecture. The three labelled regions require completely different study designs; a study designed for one is nearly blind to the others.


This figure is also a history of the field:

1980s–90s family linkage studies → the top-left corner (Mendelian disease)
2007 onwards GWAS → the bottom-right (common variants, tiny effects)
The middle → needed dense imputation and biobank-scale samples; still being filled in

💡 Reference resource — gnomAD aggregates allele frequencies across hundreds of thousands of exomes and tens of thousands of genomes, stratified by ancestry. Asking “is this variant rare?” requires specifying in which population.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
3) Germline vs. somatic









Germline
Somatic




Present in
Every cell
A subset of cells


Inherited
Yes
No


Allele fraction
~0.5 or ~1.0
Anything from <0.01 to 1.0


Control needed
Reference genome
Matched normal tissue from the same person


Typical depth
30×
100–500×, sometimes more



The analytical consequence:

Germline caller — expects clean 50/50 or 100/0 allele fractions
Somatic caller — must separate a real mutation in 3% of cells from a sequencing error in 3% of reads
→ why tumour sequencing needs far greater depth and a matched normal

title: W2. Genomics
text:
1) The conceptual pipeline
FASTQ  →  align to reference  →  BAM
       →  call variants per sample
       →  joint genotyping across the cohort
       →  quality filtering
       →  VCF
Two steps deserve comment:

Joint calling — analyses all samples together rather than one at a time

Distinguishes “homozygous reference here” from “no coverage here”
→ a distinction invisible in a single-sample VCF (🔗 W1 §2.2③)

Filtering — where most of the judgement lives

Callers produce far more candidates than are real
Criteria: coverage, strand balance, mapping quality, position within the read
⚠️ Different filter settings → meaningfully different variant sets from identical data

title: W2. Genomics
text:
2) ⚠️ Variant calls are probabilities






WarningThe most important idea in this section





A VCF looks like a list of facts. It is a list of inferences, each with a confidence — and the confidence varies enormously across the genome.
High accuracy — unique, well-covered sequence
Falls sharply in:

Repetitive and segmentally duplicated regions
GC-extreme regions with poor capture or amplification
Homopolymer runs (indel errors)
Highly polymorphic loci such as HLA — reads from divergent haplotypes align badly

→ Benchmarking resources such as Genome in a Bottle exist precisely because “accuracy” is not one number. It is a map.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
3) Choosing a platform



The same locus, three technologies. Coverage patterns are schematic but the qualitative differences are real.












WGS
WES
Array




Genome covered
~100%
~1–2% (coding)
~0.02% (selected sites)


Detects novel variants
✅
✅ (coding only)
❌


Structural variants
Partially (well with long reads)
Poorly
Large CNVs only


Non-coding regulatory variants
✅
❌
Via imputation only


Relative cost per sample
High
Medium
Very low


Typical use
Deep characterization, rare disease, SVs
Rare disease, clinical panels
GWAS, biobanks









TipWhy arrays still dominate GWAS





An array measures only pre-selected sites → cannot discover anything new. Still the workhorse of population genetics:

GWAS needs hundreds of thousands of samples far more than it needs complete genomes
The sites an array misses can be recovered statistically

→ which brings us to imputation.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
4) Imputation
The premise — nearby variants are inherited together in blocks (§3.6). Measuring one tells you a lot about its neighbours.
The method — genotypes at 500,000 array sites + a reference panel of densely sequenced genomes → statistically infer genotypes at tens of millions of unmeasured sites.

Reference panels — 1000 Genomes, HRC, TOPMed. Larger and more diverse → better imputation, especially for rarer variants
Quality score — INFO or r². Conventionally variants below 0.3–0.8 are dropped







WarningImputation quality is not uniform





Works well — common variants, in populations well represented in the reference panel
Works poorly — rare variants; ancestries under-represented in the panel, which historically has meant most of the world
An imputed genotype is a prediction. Treating predictions as measurements is how spurious associations enter the literature.
🗺️ Reference bias in its most consequential form (🔗 W1 §2.3③).

title: W2. Genomics
text:
1) Study designs



Design
Outcome
Notes




Case–control
Binary (disease / no disease)
Effect reported as odds ratio


Quantitative trait
Continuous (BMI, blood pressure, lipid level)
Usually better powered per sample


Biobank / PheWAS
Thousands of phenotypes at once
One genotype set, many outcomes (§6)



The core logic is unchanged across designs: for each variant, ask whether genotype associates with phenotype — repeat several million times.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
2) Population structure and ancestry

① PCA on genotypes

PCA on a genotype matrix recovers ancestry almost perfectly, because allele frequencies differ systematically between populations
→ the top PCs are the standard way to describe and adjust for it




Left: genotype PCA separates continental ancestries without being told about them. Right: what happens when ancestry is not balanced between cases and controls.




② Ancestry as a confounder
🔗 W1 §4.3’s confounding problem, in its classic genetic form.

Cases and controls differ in ancestry
→ every variant whose frequency differs between those ancestries shows an association
→ with no causal relationship at all

The standard defence:

Include the top ~10 genotype PCs as covariates, or
Use a mixed model accounting for genetic relatedness directly

⚠️ Neither is perfect. Residual structure — especially fine-scale structure within a country — remains a live problem.






WarningThe Eurocentric bias of human genetics





A large majority of GWAS participants to date are of European ancestry, far out of proportion to the global population. The consequences compound:

Reference panels impute non-European genomes worse
Discovered associations are tagged by European LD patterns → do not transfer
Polygenic scores lose most of their accuracy across ancestries (§5.3③)
Clinical variant databases misclassify variants that are common and benign in under-studied populations

Not only an equity problem — a validity problem. A science built on one population does not generalize, and we cannot tell how badly until we test.
💡 GWAS Diversity Monitor for the current numbers.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
3) The association test
For each variant independently, fit something close to:
\[
\text{phenotype} \sim \text{genotype} + \text{age} + \text{sex} + \text{PC}_1 + \dots + \text{PC}_{10}
\]

Genotype coded 0/1/2 — the count of the effect allele → assumes an additive model
Usually reasonable, almost always assumed
⚠️ Does mean recessive effects are detected inefficiently

Modern practice — linear mixed models (BOLT-LMM, SAIGE, REGENIE):

handle relatedness and population structure jointly
better calibrated for the extremely unbalanced case-control ratios typical of biobanks

title: W2. Genomics
text:
4) Reading the two standard figures

① Manhattan plot



Each point is one variant. Points cluster into towers because neighbouring variants are correlated, not because many independent variants are associated.


What to look at, in order:

Are there towers? → isolated single points above the line are usually artifacts, not findings
How wide are they? → a genuine signal has a shoulder of supporting variants
Which chromosomes? → a hit at chr6 ~30 Mb is the HLA region, which behaves unlike anywhere else
Is the noise floor flat? → a rising baseline suggests inflation. Check the QQ plot



② QQ plot
Observed vs. expected p-values. Under the null → points follow the diagonal.



Left: a healthy study. Right: a study whose p-values cannot be trusted as reported.


λ — the genomic inflation factor. Median observed test statistic ÷ its expected value.

λ ≈ 1 → calibrated
λ > 1.1 → a problem: unmodelled population structure, cryptic relatedness, or technical batch effects







TipAlways ask for the QQ plot





A Manhattan plot but no QQ plot is worth noticing.

A Manhattan plot cannot tell you whether the p-values are calibrated
An inflated study produces a beautiful Manhattan plot full of nothing

title: W2. Genomics
text:
5) Where 5×10⁻⁸ comes from
Not arbitrary.

~one million effectively independent common variants in European-ancestry genomes
millions of variants, but correlated in blocks → far fewer independent tests
Bonferroni:

\[
\alpha = \frac{0.05}{10^6} = 5 \times 10^{-8}
\]
Two implications students routinely miss:

It is a Bonferroni correction, not FDR. GWAS demands near-certainty per hit because follow-up costs are enormous (🔗 W1 §4.2)
⚠️ It was calibrated for European LD structure. African-ancestry genomes have shorter LD blocks → more independent tests → a stricter threshold is appropriate. An adjustment often not made

title: W2. Genomics
text:
6) Linkage disequilibrium
LD — the non-random association between alleles at nearby loci. The statistical footprint of chromosomes being inherited in segments, broken up gradually by recombination.
Simultaneously what makes GWAS possible and what makes it hard to interpret:

✅ Genotype 500,000 sites → effectively survey millions, because each measured variant tags its neighbours
⚠️ A signal appears → every variant in the block shows it, and the association statistic cannot distinguish the causal one from its correlated neighbours

title: W2. Genomics
section: 1) The lead SNP is usually not causal
text:
1) The lead SNP is usually not causal



A single GWAS “hit” at higher resolution. Colour encodes LD (r²) with the lead SNP.



Lead SNP — the variant with the smallest p-value
= the one that happened to be best measured and best tagged
= the top of the tower, not necessarily the cause

⚠️ Under realistic conditions the causal variant is frequently not the lead SNP.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
2) Fine-mapping and credible sets
Fine-mapping asks — given the association statistics and local LD structure, what is the posterior probability that each variant in this region is causal?
Output: a credible set — the smallest set of variants collectively containing the causal variant with, say, 95% probability. Honest about uncertainty in a way a single lead SNP is not.

Favourable case (strong signal, weak local LD, diverse cohort) → 1–5 variants
Unfavourable case → hundreds. Itself informative: this locus is not resolvable with current data
Cross-ancestry fine-mapping helps substantially — LD patterns differ between populations, so the intersection is narrower

title: W2. Genomics
text:
3) ⚠️ Two persistent errors






Warning“The hit is in gene X”





~90% of GWAS associations lie outside protein-coding sequence — in enhancers, promoters, untranslated regions.
→ which is why W3 (Epigenomics) exists as a chapter.
A non-coding hit does not mean a weak finding. It means the mechanism is regulatory.









Warning“So the causal gene is the nearest one”





Enhancers routinely skip over intervening genes to reach their target.
The canonical example — the FTO obesity locus:

associated variants sit inside an intron of FTO
functional work showed the causal effect operates on IRX3 and IRX5
hundreds of kilobases away

→ The nearest gene is a reasonable prior, not a conclusion.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
4) Variant to gene: the toolkit



Approach
Question
Limitation




eQTL mapping
Which variants associate with expression of which genes?
Tissue- and cell-type-specific; needs the right tissue


Colocalization
Do the GWAS and eQTL signals share the same causal variant?
Statistically distinguishes shared cause from coincidence — but low power


TWAS
Which genes’ predicted expression associates with the trait?
Efficient screen; does not establish causality


Chromatin contact
Which promoter physically contacts this enhancer?
Contact ≠ function (🔗 W3 §4.3)


CRISPR perturbation
Does editing this element change the gene?
The strongest evidence; low throughput



💡 Open Targets Genetics aggregates most of these into a single per-locus view. A good first stop for any hit.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
1) Twin heritability vs. SNP heritability
Heritability (h²) — the proportion of phenotypic variance in a population attributable to genetic variance.
Two things to hold onto:

⚠️ A population quantity, not an individual one. “Height is 80% heritable” says nothing about how much of your height is genetic
⚠️ Context-dependent. Rises when the environment is uniform, falls when it varies → the same trait can have different heritability in different populations or eras









Estimate
From
Typically




Twin h²
Comparing MZ and DZ twin similarity
Highest; includes all genetic variation, and inflates if shared-environment assumptions fail


SNP h²
Genome-wide relatedness among unrelated individuals
Lower; captures only what common SNPs tag


h² from genome-wide significant hits
Summing effects of significant loci
Lowest by far

title: W2. Genomics
text:
2) Missing heritability
For height:

Twin studies → ~80%
SNP-based estimates → ~50%
Genome-wide significant loci when GWAS began → a few percent

That gap was named the missing heritability problem and drove a decade of work. Much of it is now accounted for:

Many more, smaller effects — sample sizes into the millions → thousands of loci appeared. The variants were always there, below the detection threshold
Rare variants poorly tagged by arrays
Overestimated twin heritability — shared environment misattributed to genes

The resulting picture — polygenicity. Common traits influenced by thousands to tens of thousands of variants, most with effects too small to ever be individually meaningful.
The omnigenic model pushes this further:

in the relevant cell type, essentially any expressed gene can nudge a complex trait through the regulatory network
→ architecture dominated by a diffuse periphery rather than a core set of pathway genes

title: W2. Genomics
text:
3) Polygenic risk scores

① How a PRS is built
\[
\text{PRS}_i = \sum_{j} \hat{\beta}_j \cdot g_{ij}
\]
Each variant’s effect size \(\hat{\beta}_j\) (from a large external GWAS) × that person’s genotype \(g_{ij}\), summed.
The methodological work lies in:

handling LD so correlated variants are not counted repeatedly
shrinking noisy effect estimates
→ the job of LDpred2, PRS-CS, lassosum



② What the numbers mean



The same polygenic score, presented two ways. Both panels are correct; they leave very different impressions.



AUC ~0.65 = typical of a good PRS for a common complex disease
Also means the distributions overlap almost entirely — most cases and most controls have unremarkable scores

→ A PRS is a population-level risk stratifier, not a diagnostic test.






WarningHow PRS performance gets oversold





Three moves to watch for:

Extreme-decile contrasts — “top 10% have 7-fold higher risk than the bottom 10%” describes the same score as “AUC 0.67”. Only one sounds actionable
Relative risk without absolute risk — threefold higher risk of a disease with 0.1% baseline prevalence is 0.3%
Evaluation in the discovery population — performance always drops in an independent cohort, and drops further across ancestries






③ ⚠️ Portability
A score derived in one ancestry, applied to another → accuracy degrades substantially. Commonly retaining only a fraction of its original performance in African-ancestry individuals.
The causes are cumulative:

different allele frequencies
different LD patterns → tag SNPs no longer tag
different effect sizes
different environmental context

⚠️ Deploying European-derived PRS clinically without addressing this would systematically widen health disparities. The single most important open problem in the clinical translation of PRS.

title: W2. Genomics
text:
1) Cancer genomics in brief
Cancer is a somatic genetic disease → different questions.

Driver vs. passenger — a tumour genome carries thousands of mutations; a handful drive proliferation, the rest are bystanders. Distinguishing them is a statistical problem: drivers recur across patients more often than the background mutation rate predicts
Mutational signatures — different mutagenic processes leave characteristic patterns (UV, tobacco, APOBEC, mismatch repair deficiency). Decomposing a tumour’s spectrum into COSMIC signatures can reveal aetiology and sometimes a therapeutic vulnerability
TMB and MSI as biomarkers — both index how many neoantigens a tumour presents; both predict response to immune checkpoint blockade well enough to have supported tissue-agnostic regulatory approvals

title: W2. Genomics
text:
2) Mendelian randomization in one page
The problem — observational epidemiology cannot separate causation from confounding and reverse causation.
The instrument — genetic variants. Alleles are assigned at conception and are not influenced by lifestyle or disease status → an association between a genetically predicted exposure and an outcome is much harder to explain by confounding.
Three required assumptions:

The variant genuinely affects the exposure
It is not associated with confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship
⚠️ It affects the outcome only through the exposure — the one that fails most often, because of pleiotropy (one variant affecting many traits)

Track record:

✅ Most convincing where it confirms and quantifies causal roles that trials later validated — e.g. LDL cholesterol in coronary disease
⚠️ Least convincing where assumption ③ is doubtful

title: W2. Genomics
text:
3) 💊 Genetics for drug discovery
The problem — most drug candidates fail in clinical development, and the commonest reason is lack of efficacy: the target was not causal for the disease.
What genetics contributes — evidence on exactly that question.

Analyses of development pipelines: targets with supporting human genetic evidence are roughly twice as likely to succeed
→ reorganized target selection across the pharmaceutical industry
→ a large part of why GWAS continues to be funded at scale

Retrospective validation:

PCSK9 loss-of-function carriers → low LDL, low cardiovascular risk → anticipated PCSK9 inhibitors
HMGCR variants → recapitulate the effects of statins

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
1) Bio + Information
A compound word, and both halves matter.

Bio ➡️ human samples, cells, tissues — with phenotypes attached
Information ➡️ data, usually omics data, usually a very large table




Bioinformatics sits at the intersection of biology, computer science, and statistics — and spans the whole path from sample to interpretation.


The job — turn the second into a statement about the first.
The difficulty — the translation is lossy in both directions:

A tumour ➡️ a matrix of numbers
A matrix of numbers ➡️ a claim about a tumour

Most of this course is about where information leaks out at each step.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
2) Three neighbouring fields
Often used interchangeably. Different jobs.








Field
Central question
Typical output




Bioinformatics
How do I get from raw data to an interpretable measurement?
Processed matrices, variant calls, annotated gene lists


Computational biology
Can I build a model that explains or predicts biology?
Simulations, predictive models, mechanistic theory


Biostatistics
Given this design, what can I legitimately conclude?
Estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, study designs



In practice one person does all three. The distinction matters when deciding who to ask:

“My aligner is throwing away 40% of reads” → bioinformatics
“Is n = 3 enough?” → biostatistics, and it should have been asked months earlier







TipThe most useful thing you will learn this semester





Not how to run anything.
Recognizing which of those three questions you are actually asking — because asking the wrong specialist wastes months.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
3) Wet lab ➡️ dry lab
You already have the right reflexes. A beautiful Western blot prompts: what was the loading control? how many biological replicates? was the exposure saturated?
Same reflexes, different artifacts:







Wet lab habit
Dry lab equivalent




Loading control
Normalization (W4)


Antibody validation
Reference database / annotation choice (W1, W6)


Blinding and randomization
Batch design and randomized sample layout (W1)


Technical vs. biological replicate
The same distinction, more consequential (W4)


“It worked once”
A finding that does not replicate in a second cohort



The failure mode unique to computation — the analysis always produces an answer.

Failed PCR → an empty gel. Obvious
Failed RNA-seq analysis → a tidy table of 847 genes, sorted by p-value. Nothing about its appearance tells you it is wrong

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
4) The generic omics workflow 🗺️
The omics layers of the next six weeks, organized by the central dogma — each with its own characteristic question.



W2 works on the genome, W3 on its regulatory state, W4–W5 on the transcriptome, W6 on the proteome. W7 asks the same questions of a second genome — the microbiome.


Every analysis in this course — genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metagenomics — follows the same five stages.
① Quality control     → is this data usable at all?
② Alignment /          → where did each measurement come from,
   quantification         and how much of it is there?
③ Normalization       → make samples comparable to each other
④ Statistical testing → which differences are larger than noise?
⑤ Interpretation      → what does that mean biologically?






ImportantThis is the map for the whole course





Every week from W2 onward: ask where in these five stages you are. The technologies differ enormously; the stages barely change.
The stages are also where the errors live — and they are not equally dangerous:

Stage ① ② errors → loud. The pipeline crashes, or the numbers are absurd
Stage ③ ④ errors → quiet. These are the ones that reach publication

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
1) Sequencing technologies in one hour
Nearly all omics data here comes from sequencing DNA — even when the question is about RNA, chromatin, or protein binding. The trick that made omics possible: convert every molecular question into “count the DNA fragments.”
The other enabler was economics — cost per genome fell faster than Moore’s law, from ~$100 million in 2001 to a few hundred dollars today.



Cost per human genome. The discontinuity around 2007–2008 is the arrival of massively parallel short-read sequencing. Source: NHGRI.








NoteWhy this graph matters for you






Then — the bottleneck was generating data
Now — the bottleneck is interpreting it, and increasingly, having a design worth interpreting

That shift is the entire reason this course exists.




① Sanger sequencing

chain termination with fluorescently labelled ddNTPs


The original method; still the clinical gold standard for confirming a single variant
One reaction = one template, up to ~800–1,000 bases
Very high per-base accuracy




Sanger sequencing. A ddNTP lacks the 3′-OH needed for the next phosphodiester bond, so incorporation terminates the chain. A ladder of fragments of every length, each labelled by its terminal base, reads out the sequence.


⚠️ The limitation is throughput, not quality. One gene is trivial. One genome took thirteen years and ~$3 billion.


② Short-read sequencing (Illumina)

massively parallel sequencing by synthesis

The key idea — parallelism. Not one molecule read well, but hundreds of millions read simultaneously, each moderately well.
The workflow:

Library preparation — fragment the DNA, ligate adapters to both ends
Cluster generation — each fragment amplified in place on a flow cell
Sequencing by synthesis — one fluorescent, reversibly terminated base per cycle: add, image, unblock; repeat 50–300×




Left: library preparation — fragmentation, adapter ligation, denaturation. Right: bridge amplification on the flow cell, which turns one molecule into a cluster bright enough to image.



The library molecule
Everything entering the sequencer: adapter + insert + adapter. Each component has a job.



P5/P7 bind the flow cell. Rd1/Rd2 SP are the sequencing primer binding sites. Index1/Index2 identify the sample.


Two features matter for interpretation:

Index (barcode) — 6–12 nt, identifies the sample

Enables multiplexing: many samples in one lane, demultiplexed afterwards
⚠️ Also where sample swaps and index hopping happen — reads assigned to the wrong sample. Dual indexing exists because single indexing was not reliable enough

Single-end vs. paired-end — reading the fragment from one end or both




Single-end gives one read per fragment; paired-end gives two, with a known approximate distance between them. That distance is what lets an aligner place reads confidently in repetitive regions and detect splice junctions and rearrangements.



Paired-end costs more → better alignment in repeats, plus structural rearrangements and splice junctions (🔗 W4)
Typical output today: 2 × 150 bp, per-base error ~0.1%
⚠️ Read length is the fundamental limit — 150 bases is shorter than most repeats, most structural variants, and most full-length transcripts




③ Long-read sequencing (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore)

read the whole molecule, accept more errors per base


PacBio HiFi — circular template read repeatedly, consensus taken. ~15–25 kb reads, accuracy comparable to short reads
Oxford Nanopore — single strand threaded through a protein pore, ionic current decoded

Reads can exceed a megabase
Raw accuracy below Illumina, though modern chemistries have narrowed the gap considerably
Detects base modifications (e.g. DNA methylation) directly, without bisulfite conversion (🔗 W3)




④ The trade-off triangle
Read length, per-base accuracy, cost per base — you cannot maximize all three. Every platform picks a corner.











Read length
Accuracy
Cost / Gb
Best for




Sanger
~800 bp
Very high
Very high
Confirming a single variant


Illumina
50–300 bp
High
Low
Counting: RNA-seq, ChIP, WGS/WES at scale


PacBio HiFi
15–25 kb
High
Moderate
Assembly, structural variants, phasing


Nanopore
up to Mb
Moderate
Moderate
Ultra-long spans, direct modification calling, portability









TipThe question to ask about any dataset





Not “which platform?” but “is the read long enough to answer my question?”

Variant in a segmental duplication? → 150 bp reads will not save you
Transcript with ten isoforms differing at the 3′ end? → same

No amount of depth fixes a read-length problem.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
2) The shape of biological data
You will probably never open these files by hand — but you will read methods sections that mention them, and reviewers will ask.
What matters: what each format holds, and what it has already thrown away.

① FASTQ — the raw read
Four lines per read, tens of millions of reads per sample.
@SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51           ← read ID
GCCTTGGTGGTGAAATGGTAGACTGGAATTCTCGGGTGCC   ← sequence
+SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51           ← description
F:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFF   ← base quality (Phred)

Knows — the sequence, and the machine’s confidence in each base
Does not know — where in the genome the read came from. That information does not exist yet


Phred quality score
\[Q = -10 \log_{10} P\]
where \(P\) = probability that the base call is wrong.



Phred score
Error rate
Base call accuracy




10
1 in 10
90%


20
1 in 100
99%


30
1 in 1,000
99.9%


40
1 in 10,000
99.99%



Q30 = the conventional benchmark. “>80% of bases above Q30” is the sort of line you will see in a facility report.



② BAM — reads placed on a genome
Every read + the coordinate the aligner assigned + a mapping quality for that assignment.
⚠️ Alignment is inference, not observation.

A read from a repetitive region could plausibly come from several places
The aligner picks one and lowers the mapping quality to say so
Analyses that ignore mapping quality silently accept a lot of wrong placements

BAM is where read-level information ends for most projects — large (tens of GB per WGS sample), and everything downstream is a summary of it.


③ VCF — differences from a reference
Positions where your sample differs from the reference, with genotype and quality. Everything shared with the reference is implicit and absent.
⚠️ A VCF is a diff, not a genome.

A region that could not be aligned produces no variants
That looks identical to a region with no variants
Absence of a call ≠ a call of absence



④ Count matrix — where most analyses actually begin
Features (genes, peaks, proteins, taxa) in rows × samples in columns, one number per cell.

What public repositories distribute, and what statistical methods consume
Also the point of maximum information loss — every read, alignment, and quality score compressed into one integer per gene per sample







WarningWhat the count matrix has already decided for you





By the time it reaches you, someone has already chosen:

Reference genome build
Annotation version
Aligner
Quantification method
Rules for multi-mapping reads

All invisible in the matrix. All capable of changing your results substantially.
→ Download a matrix from GEO, and the original paper’s methods section is part of your methods section.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
3) The reference genome

① GRCh38 and T2T-CHM13
Not a person’s genome — a mosaic from several donors, curated over two decades. An idealized coordinate system everyone agrees to use.

GRCh38 (2013) — the workhorse. Still the default for most clinical and population resources, largely because enormous datasets are already mapped to it
T2T-CHM13 (2022) — the first genuinely complete assembly: centromeres, acrocentric short arms, and other GRCh38 gaps. Adds ~200 Mb of previously unmapped sequence
Pangenome references — a graph of many haplotypes rather than one linear sequence. Where the field is heading; not yet the default

⚠️ Coordinates are not interchangeable between builds.

A position in GRCh37 (hg19) is a different position in GRCh38
“Liftover” is routine but lossy
Mixing builds is one of the commonest sources of nonsense results in student projects



② Annotation: where the genes are

Reference sequence — what the bases are
Annotation — which stretches are genes, exons, transcripts, regulatory elements

Separate files, separately versioned, and they disagree with each other.

GENCODE — comprehensive; used by ENCODE and GTEx. Includes many lncRNAs and predicted transcripts
RefSeq — NCBI’s conservative, manually curated set. Standard in clinical reporting

~20,000 protein-coding genes — a remarkably stable number. But transcript counts differ by tens of thousands between sources and versions.






WarningAnnotation version is a hidden variable





Same FASTQ files + different GENCODE release →

different gene counts
different library totals
→ different normalization factors
→ different DE results

Usually modest differences. Occasionally not.
Report the build and the annotation version. Every time.





③ Reference bias
Everything is measured relative to one sequence → anything poorly represented in that sequence is systematically under-detected.

Divergent haplotypes — reads from non-European-ancestry individuals map slightly worse to a reference built mostly from European donors → subtle allele-frequency and coverage biases (🔗 W2)
Highly polymorphic loci — HLA is the classic case; standard alignment badly misrepresents it
Repetitive and duplicated regions — reads map ambiguously or not at all
Sequence absent from the reference — undetectable by definition

🗺️ First appearance of a thread running through the whole course: reference bias.

W3 → chromatin atlases
W4 → annotation versions
W6 → the protein search database
W7 → the 16S taxonomy database

Same problem, different name.
