title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
section: 4) 💡 What makes a public dataset worth reanalyzing
text:
4) 💡 What makes a public dataset worth reanalyzing
Not all deposited data is usable. Check before committing a semester to a GEO accession:

✅ Sample size — n > 30 per group for most bulk questions. Small studies are underpowered no matter how clean
✅ Clear design — unambiguous case vs. control, or a paired design (stronger: within-patient variation is controlled statistically)
✅ Rich metadata — age, sex, batch, tissue, treatment. A matrix without covariates cannot be corrected for confounding
✅ Raw data available — reprocessing with your own annotation needs the FASTQs, not just the matrix
⚠️ Batch structure recoverable — all cases in one batch and all controls in another → unsalvageable. This is common. Check first

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
section: 1) What a p-value does and does not say
text:
1) What a p-value does and does not say
Is — the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. That is all.
Is not —

the probability that the null hypothesis is true
the probability that your finding will replicate
a measure of effect size
any statement about biological importance

Two illustrations:

n = 200 per group → a 3% expression difference can reach p < 0.001 and mean nothing
n = 3 → a genuine two-fold change can fail to reach significance

→ Always read the effect size alongside the p-value.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
2) Multiple testing

One gene at α = 0.05 → 5% chance of a false positive
20,000 genes, no real signal at all → ~1,000 false positives expected

Two corrections dominate:









Method
Controls
Behaviour
Use when




Bonferroni
Family-wise error rate — P(≥1 false positive)
Very conservative
You need near-certainty about every hit (e.g. GWAS, 🔗 W2)


Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR)
Expected proportion of false positives among hits
Much more permissive
Screening / discovery (e.g. RNA-seq, 🔗 W4)



FDR is the omics default — the goal is usually a ranked candidate list for follow-up, not individually certain claims.
“FDR < 0.05” = about 5% of the genes on this list are expected to be false.

Acceptable bargain when the next step is validation
Unacceptable when the next step is a clinical decision







WarningThe correction cannot be applied after the fact






Tested 20,000 genes, found one interesting result, reported only that one with an uncorrected p-value? → you have not avoided the multiple testing problem, you have hidden it
Tried six normalization methods and reported the one with the nicest volcano plot? → also multiple testing, and no correction exists for it

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
3) Batch effects and confounding ⚠️
Batch effect — systematic technical variation between groups of samples processed together: different days, reagent lots, flow cells, technicians, extraction kits.
In omics it is routinely larger than the biological effect you are looking for.
Batch effects are annoying but survivable. Confounding is fatal:
Recoverable:   Batch 1 = 5 cases + 5 controls
               Batch 2 = 5 cases + 5 controls
               → batch can be modelled and removed

Unrecoverable: Batch 1 = 10 cases
               Batch 2 = 10 controls
               → batch and disease are the same variable
                 no statistical method can separate them
In the second case:

every method that removes the batch effect also removes your signal
every method that preserves the signal preserves the artifact
→ the experiment cannot be rescued by analysis. It has to be redesigned







ImportantRandomize your sample layout





Costs nothing. Prevents the single most common unrecoverable error in omics studies.
When laying samples on a plate or submitting for sequencing, distribute conditions evenly across every technical grouping — plate, row, run, day, operator.
If you take one practical thing from this chapter, take this one.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
4) Power, effect size, and n
Statistical power — the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size.
Depends on: effect size · variability · n · and in omics, the multiple testing burden (the threshold is far stricter than 0.05).
Rough orientation, not rules:

Bulk RNA-seq — n = 3 detects only large, consistent changes. n = 6–10 is a working minimum for human tissue. n > 20 for clinically heterogeneous phenotypes
GWAS — thousands to hundreds of thousands; individual variant effects are tiny (🔗 W2)
Single-cell — the relevant n is the number of donors, not cells. Three donors is three, whether you sequenced 300 cells or 300,000 (🔗 W5)







WarningUnderpowered studies are worse than no study





They do not simply fail to find things. What they do find is:

enriched for false positives
systematically inflated in effect size — only the largest apparent effects survive the significance filter

→ why small pilot studies so often fail to replicate at their reported effect size.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
section: 1) Why the same data gives different answers
text:
1) Why the same data gives different answers
Identical FASTQ files → two competent analysts → two different gene lists. Overlap is usually good, rarely complete.
The divergence accumulates from individually reasonable choices:

Reference build and annotation version
Aligner and its parameters
Handling of multi-mapping reads
Filtering thresholds for low-expression features
Normalization method
The statistical model, and which covariates it includes
Significance and effect-size thresholds

None of these is wrong. But there are enough of them that a determined analyst can reach almost any conclusion — usually without realizing it, by stopping when the result looks biologically sensible.






TipThe defense






Decide the analysis plan before seeing the results
Write it down
Explore if you must — but label exploratory findings as exploratory

Standard practice in clinical trials for exactly this reason. Omics is at least as vulnerable.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
section: 2) What a good methods section contains
text:
2) What a good methods section contains
You will write these, and you will review them.

✅ Reference build and annotation version, with release numbers
✅ Every tool with its version number
✅ Non-default parameters
✅ Filtering criteria — how many features and samples removed, and why
✅ The full statistical model, including covariates
✅ Multiple testing correction method and threshold
✅ Accession numbers for data, and a link to analysis code

❌ “Data were analyzed using standard pipelines” is not a methods section. You will see it in print constantly.

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
section: 3) 🗣️ The conversation to have before you sequence
text:
3) 🗣️ The conversation to have before you sequence
The highest-value section of this chapter. Most analysis problems are design problems that became visible too late.
Agree on these before samples leave your bench:







Question
Why it matters




What is the comparison?
Determines the whole design. “Let’s see what’s different” is not a comparison


How many biological replicates?
The single biggest determinant of what you can detect


What is the unit of replication?
Patients? Mice? Wells? Cells? This is where n is usually overstated


What covariates will we need?
Age, sex, batch, RIN, cell composition. Collect them now; you cannot add them later


How will samples be laid out?
Randomize across batches. Non-negotiable


What are the technical constraints?
Read length, depth, single vs. paired-end — driven by the question, not the price list


Is there a validation plan?
An orthogonal assay, or an independent cohort. Reviewers will ask









ImportantAsk your analyst one question





“Given this design, what would I be able to conclude if the experiment works perfectly?”
If the honest answer is “not much” — you have just saved yourself a year, before spending anything.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what RNA-seq measures and what it does not
Choose between poly(A) selection and rRNA depletion for a given question
Explain why raw counts cannot be compared, and what each normalisation corrects
Explain why count data needs a negative binomial model rather than a t-test
Read a volcano plot and an MA plot, and say which is the better diagnostic
Distinguish ORA from GSEA and name the three commonest misuses of enrichment analysis
⚠️ Recognize when a “differential expression” result is really a change in cell composition

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
1) Steady-state abundance, not synthesis
RNA-seq counts the transcripts present at the moment you lysed the sample.

That number = the balance of two rates: transcription and degradation
⚠️ The assay cannot separate them
→ a gene whose transcription doubles and a gene whose mRNA half-life doubles look identical

If the distinction matters to your hypothesis, you need a different assay:

Nascent transcription — GRO-seq, TT-seq
Metabolic labelling — SLAM-seq
Translation — ribosome profiling

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
2) ⚠️ RNA is not protein

Transcript and protein abundance correlate at r ≈ 0.4 across genes
A real correlation — and nowhere near enough to treat mRNA as a proxy for protein for any individual gene

Missing from RNA-seq: translation efficiency, protein half-life, post-translational regulation. 🔗 W6 takes this up properly.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) A snapshot, of a mixture
Two further limits, worth stating early:

⚠️ One time point — transcriptional responses are dynamic. A single harvest can miss an effect entirely, or catch a transient one and misread it as steady state
⚠️ A mixture of cells — bulk RNA-seq averages over every cell in the tube. §7.2 shows how badly that misleads; 🔗 W5 is the response




The bench workflow. Every decision on this line constrains what the analysis can do.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
1) Poly(A) selection vs. rRNA depletion
Ribosomal RNA = ~80–90% of total RNA in a cell. Sequence total RNA directly → most of your budget buys rRNA. Every protocol removes it, one of two ways.



Where the reads go, and how to choose.



Poly(A) selection — oligo-dT beads capture transcripts with a poly(A) tail. Clean, cheap, the default for DE studies
rRNA depletion — complementary probes remove rRNA, keep everything else: non-polyadenylated transcripts, nascent unspliced RNA, degraded fragments







TipWhich to choose






Standard mRNA DE, good-quality RNA → poly(A)
FFPE or degraded RNA → rRNA depletion. Poly(A) selection fails, because degraded transcripts have lost their tails
lncRNA, circRNA, histone mRNAs, nascent transcription → rRNA depletion

⚠️ Made at the bench. Cannot be undone in analysis.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
2) Stranded vs. unstranded

A stranded protocol records which strand the original transcript came from
~10–20% of the genome has overlapping transcription on both strands → without strand information those reads are assigned ambiguously or wrongly
→ stranded is now standard, and there is little reason not to use it

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) Read length, depth, and paired-end



Choice
When it matters




Longer reads (2×150 vs 1×50)
Isoform and splice junction work; less benefit for plain gene-level counting


Paired-end
Isoforms, fusion detection, novel transcripts. For gene-level DE, single-end is often sufficient


Depth
See §5.4 — saturates much earlier than people expect

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
4) Biological vs. technical replicates

Technical replicate — the same RNA sequenced twice
Biological replicate — a different animal, patient, or independently cultured dish

⚠️ Technical variability in RNA-seq is small; biological variability is not.

Sequencing one sample twice tells you almost nothing new
→ n counts biological replicates only
Three flasks from the same passage split on the same day are closer to technical than biological, whatever the methods section calls them

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
5) ✅ Design checklist
Before samples leave the bench (🔗 W1 §5.3):

✅ Randomise across batches — extraction day, library prep batch, sequencing run. All cases in batch 1 and all controls in batch 2 → unrecoverable
✅ Record RIN and treat it as a covariate. RNA quality shifts measurements systematically
✅ Record everything else you might need to adjust for — age, sex, tissue site, time of collection
✅ Decide n before you start (§5.4)
✅ Keep the design balanced — unbalanced designs are analysable but lose power fast

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
1) Spliced alignment
The problem — reads come from mature mRNA, but you align to a genome. A read crossing an exon–exon junction will not align contiguously.
The fix — spliced aligners (STAR, HISAT2) allow large gaps at annotated or novel junctions.
Use this route when read position matters: novel transcripts, splicing, fusions, allele-specific expression, or anything you want to view in a genome browser.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
2) Pseudo-alignment
Salmon and kallisto skip base-level alignment. They ask only which transcripts a read is compatible with, then resolve the assignment statistically across all reads.

✅ ~an order of magnitude faster, far less memory
✅ transcript-level estimates at least as accurate for quantification
❌ no BAM file → cannot inspect alignments
❌ can only quantify transcripts already in the annotation

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) Gene level vs. transcript level

Most genes produce several isoforms
Transcript-level quantification → more informative, but noisier: reads shared between isoforms must be probabilistically assigned

💡 The pragmatic standard — quantify at transcript level, then sum to gene level (the tximport route). Gene-level results are more robust, and you keep the option of looking at isoforms later.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
4) Multi-mapping reads
Reads mapping equally well to several places — paralogues, repeats, pseudogenes — must be handled somehow:

Discard → systematically under-counts gene families
Distribute probabilistically → better, but introduces its own uncertainty

⚠️ One of the invisible decisions baked into any count matrix you download from GEO (🔗 W1 §2.2④).

title: W4. Transcriptomics
section: 1) Why raw counts cannot be compared
text:
1) Why raw counts cannot be compared
A count depends on three things that have nothing to do with biology:

Library size (depth) — sequence twice as deeply → every gene doubles
Gene length — a 10 kb transcript generates more fragments than a 1 kb transcript at the same molar concentration
Library composition — the subtle one




① and ② are the obvious problem. ③ is the one that motivates TMM and RLE.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
2) ⚠️ The composition effect
Sequencing measures proportions, not absolute amounts. The total is fixed by how many reads you bought.

One gene — or a handful — becomes enormously abundant in one condition
→ it consumes a larger share of the library
→ every other gene’s proportion falls, though nothing happened to it
⚠️ Simple depth normalisation (CPM) cannot fix this, because depth is not what changed

The fix — TMM (edgeR) and RLE / median-of-ratios (DESeq2) both assume most genes are not differentially expressed, and use that majority to estimate a per-sample scaling factor.
→ why they are the standard for differential expression and CPM is not.






WarningThe assumption behind TMM and RLE





Both assume the majority of genes do not change. Usually safe.
Fails when there is a global transcriptional shift:

MYC amplification
global transcriptional shutdown
some drug treatments
comparing very different tissues

→ in those cases you need spike-in controls (ERCC) to anchor the scale.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) Which measure, when









Method
Corrects
Comparable
Use for




Raw counts
nothing
—
Input to DESeq2 / edgeR — do not pre-normalise


CPM
depth
between samples
Filtering low-expression genes


RPKM / FPKM
depth + length
within a sample only
Legacy; avoid for comparisons


TPM
depth + length
within and (loosely) between
Reporting expression levels, heatmaps


TMM / RLE
depth + composition
between samples
Differential expression — the standard









ImportantNever feed normalised values into DESeq2 or edgeR






These tools model raw counts and estimate their own size factors internally
Handing them TPM or CPM breaks the variance model
→ invalidates the p-values

A common and quiet error.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
section: 1) Why counts need a negative binomial model
text:
1) Why counts need a negative binomial model

Pure random sampling → counts would be Poisson: variance = mean. Technical replicates roughly behave this way
Biological replicates → far more variable. Overdispersed, and the excess variance grows with expression level




Left: the reason a t-test on counts produces false positives. Right: the reason n = 3 works at all.


The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter φ:
\[
\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \phi \mu^2
\]

φ = 0 → recovers Poisson
Estimating φ honestly is what separates a valid analysis from an optimistic one

title: W4. Transcriptomics
section: 2) Dispersion, shrinkage, and why n = 3 works at all
text:
2) Dispersion, shrinkage, and why n = 3 works at all
The problem — three numbers give a terrible variance estimate. You cannot estimate a gene’s variance from n = 3.
The solution — borrow information across genes:

fit a smooth trend of dispersion vs. mean expression using all genes
shrink each gene’s noisy individual estimate toward that trend

💡 The single most important methodological idea in bulk RNA-seq, and why the standard tools outperform a per-gene t-test so decisively at small n.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) The three standard tools








Tool
Model
Notes




DESeq2
Negative binomial; shrinkage of dispersion and log fold change
Conservative; good default; handles small n well


edgeR
Negative binomial; empirical Bayes dispersion
Very similar in practice; quasi-likelihood mode slightly more conservative


limma-voom
Transforms counts, models precision weights, then linear models
Fastest at large n; most flexible for complex designs



💡 In benchmark after benchmark the three agree on large-effect genes and disagree at the margins.
→ If your conclusion depends on which one you used, you do not have a conclusion.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
4) ⚠️ Sample size — the weakest link



Left: power against replicates. Right: what extra sequencing depth actually buys you.








Warningn = 3 is a convention, not a justification





Three replicates detect only large, consistent changes. For human tissue with real between-individual variability, usually insufficient.
Rough orientation:

Cell lines, clean perturbation — n = 3–4 may be acceptable
Mouse tissue — n = 5–8
Human tissue / clinical samples — n = 10–20 minimum, more if the phenotype is heterogeneous

And note the right-hand panel: depth saturates, replicates do not.

20–30 M reads per sample is enough for most DE questions
→ money spent beyond that would buy more power as additional samples

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
5) Reading a results table



Two views of the same result. Most papers show only the first.



Adjusted p-value — almost always Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (🔗 W1 §4.2). “FDR < 0.05” → ~5% of the genes on this list are expected to be false
log₂ fold change — 1 = a doubling, −1 = a halving. For small n, report DESeq2’s shrunken LFC; raw LFCs at low counts are wildly unstable
Volcano plot — significance vs. effect size. ⚠️ Both threshold lines are conventions
MA plot — effect size vs. expression level. The better diagnostic — it reveals whether your hits are concentrated at low counts, which is what a poorly controlled analysis looks like







WarningTwo habits worth breaking





① Filtering by fold change alone.

log₂FC = 3 with padj = 0.4 is not a finding
→ fold-change thresholds without significance filtering are how “top 20 gene” lists become unreproducible

② Treating the threshold as biology.

padj = 0.049 and padj = 0.051 are indistinguishable
→ report the ranked list, not just the cut

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
1) ORA vs. GSEA



Two ways to ask the same question. They are not equivalent.



ORA (over-representation analysis) — take the significant gene list, ask by Fisher’s exact test whether a pathway is over-represented relative to a background set
GSEA — take all genes ranked by some statistic, ask whether a pathway’s members cluster toward one end. No threshold applied

💡 GSEA’s specific advantage — it detects a pathway where fifty genes each shift by 1.3×. Coordinated, biologically meaningful, and completely invisible to any threshold-based method.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
2) Which databases








Resource
Content
Caution




GO
Biological process, molecular function, cellular component
Highly redundant; terms nested at wildly different specificity


KEGG
Curated metabolic and signalling pathways
Manually curated but slow to update


Reactome
Detailed, hierarchical reaction-level pathways
Deeper than KEGG, more complex to summarise


MSigDB Hallmark
50 refined, non-redundant gene sets
💡 The best starting point — designed to reduce redundancy

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) ⚠️ The three commonest misuses






WarningEnrichment analysis is easy to do and easy to do wrong





① The wrong background set.

Only 12,000 of 20,000 genes expressed in your tissue → your background is 12,000
Using the full annotation inflates every p-value in the output
→ the single most common error in the literature

② Threshold sensitivity.

padj 0.05 → 0.10 can change the top pathway entirely
→ if your headline result does not survive that, say so

③ Enrichment is not mechanism.

“Enriched for immune response” describes your gene list. It identifies no driver, no direction, no cause
⚠️ Large generic categories (immune, metabolic, cell cycle) are enriched in almost every perturbation, because they contain thousands of genes

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
1) Co-expression networks
Instead of comparing conditions → ask which genes vary together across samples.

WGCNA clusters genes into modules of correlated expression, then relates module summaries to traits
✅ Useful when there is no clean two-group comparison, and to reduce 20,000 genes to a dozen interpretable modules
⚠️ Needs many samples — 20 is a floor, 50+ is better. It is estimating a correlation structure

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
2) ⚠️ Deconvolution — the composition problem again



The same logic as W3’s cell composition confounder, in a different assay.








Warning“Neuronal genes down, microglial genes up”





Bulk expression = the weighted average of the cell types present.

Disease changes the mixture — neuron loss, immune infiltration, fibrosis
→ coherent, highly significant “differential expression”
→ without a single cell changing what it transcribes

🔗 Exactly the confounder from W3 §5.3②, in a different assay — and why so many bulk tissue studies report cell-type marker genes as their top hits.
What to do:

✅ Estimate cell type proportions computationally (CIBERSORTx, MuSiC, BayesPrism — all need a single-cell reference) → include as covariates
✅ Or measure single cells directly (🔗 W5)

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
3) Splicing and isoforms

Differential expression — did the gene’s total output change?
Differential splicing — did the proportions of its isoforms change?

The second can matter enormously with no change in the first.
Tools: DEXSeq (exon usage), rMATS and LeafCutter (splicing events).
⚠️ All need more depth and more replicates than gene-level DE. Paired-end reads help substantially.

title: W4. Transcriptomics
text:
4) Expression as a genetic trait
Bring W2 back.

eQTL — a genetic variant associated with a gene’s expression level
GTEx — eQTLs across 54 human tissues from hundreds of donors

→ the main bridge from a non-coding GWAS hit to a candidate gene (🔗 W2 §4.4).
⚠️ With a caveat that connects all three chapters so far: eQTLs are tissue- and cell-type-specific. An eQTL measured in whole blood tells you little about what a variant does in neurons.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what single-cell RNA-seq answers that bulk cannot
Choose between droplet and plate-based protocols, and between cells and nuclei
Explain what a UMI is and why the count matrix is mostly zeros
Interpret a knee plot and the standard QC scatter, and name what each artifact looks like
⚠️ Read a UMAP responsibly — and say what its distances do and do not mean
Explain why clustering resolution is arbitrary and what to check it against
⚠️ Explain why per-cell differential expression tests are invalid, and what pseudobulk does instead

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
1) What averaging destroys



One bulk measurement is compatible with all three of these. Bulk cannot tell them apart; single-cell can.


The entire argument for the technology. A bulk experiment reports the mean — and the mean is compatible with radically different biology:

① A general modest response — the least interesting case, and the one people implicitly assume
② A rare responsive subpopulation — usually the interesting case. In bulk it is diluted by the 85% of cells doing nothing, and often falls below significance entirely
③ A change in composition — no cell changed its transcriptome at all (🔗 W4 §7.2; 🔗 W3 §5.3② for the epigenomic version)

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
section: 2) What single cell is actually good at
text:
2) What single cell is actually good at
Be specific — single-cell is expensive and frequently used where bulk would answer better.
Single-cell is right for:

Discovering or characterising cell populations, including rare ones
Composition — which cell types shifted in disease
Cell-type-specific effects — a gene up in one cell type and down in another, invisible in bulk
Continuous states — differentiation, activation, exhaustion, where discrete categories fail

Bulk is still right for:

A well-defined comparison in a homogeneous system (cell line, sorted population)
Deep transcript-level work — isoforms, low-expression genes, splicing
Large cohorts — n = 200 patients, where n = 200 single-cell runs is unaffordable







TipSorting first is underrated





Already know which cell type you care about?
→ FACS-sort it and run deep bulk RNA-seq. Often cheaper, deeper, and statistically cleaner than a whole-tissue single-cell experiment.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
1) The fundamental trade-off



Every platform buys cells with depth, or depth with cells.



Droplet-based (10x Genomics) — cells captured in oil droplets with barcoded beads. Tens of thousands of cells, a few thousand genes per cell, 3′ (or 5′) end only. The current default
Plate-based (Smart-seq2/3) — one cell per well, full-length, deep. Hundreds of cells. Still the choice for isoforms or very sensitive detection
Combinatorial indexing (sci-, SPLiT-seq) — no physical isolation; barcoding through rounds of split-pool. Millions of cells, very shallow. What makes whole-organism atlases possible

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
2) ⚠️ Cells vs. nuclei
snRNA-seq profiles nuclei instead of whole cells. Not a lesser version of scRNA-seq — for many tissues it is the only option.









scRNA-seq
snRNA-seq




Frozen / archived tissue
❌ needs fresh
✅


Large or fragile cells (neurons, adipocytes, myofibres, cardiomyocytes)
❌ lost during dissociation
✅


Dissociation stress response
⚠️ Yes — immediate early genes (FOS, JUN, heat shock) induced by the protocol itself
✅ Minimal


Cytoplasmic transcripts
✅ Captured
❌ Missed


Fraction of intronic reads
Low
High — nuclei are enriched for unspliced pre-mRNA









WarningDissociation is an experiment you did not intend to run





What happens:

Enzymatic dissociation at 37 °C for 30–60 minutes
Cells are alive and responding the whole time → stress-response genes induced
⚠️ Worse — dissociation is not uniform. Neurons, adipocytes, and large or fragile cells are destroyed preferentially

→ The composition you measure is the composition that survived, not the composition of the tissue.
💡 Finding “cell type X is depleted in disease”? Ask whether cell type X is simply harder to dissociate from diseased tissue.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
1) Barcodes and UMIs
Two barcodes attached to every captured transcript:

Cell barcode — identifies the droplet, and therefore the cell
UMI (unique molecular identifier) — a random sequence unique to each original mRNA molecule

Why the UMI matters — after PCR, one original molecule may be represented by hundreds of reads. Collapsing reads that share a UMI recovers the count of molecules rather than reads → removes amplification bias.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
2) Why the matrix is >90% zeros
A typical droplet experiment detects 1,000–5,000 genes per cell, out of ~20,000.
Zeros have two very different meanings:

Biological zero — the gene really is not expressed in that cell
Technical zero (dropout) — the transcript was there but was not captured. Droplet capture efficiency is ~10–30%

💡 The field has largely moved on from calling this “zero inflation” — for UMI data the zeros are mostly what a simple sampling model predicts from low counts, not an extra process.
⚠️ The practical consequence stands: you cannot conclude a gene is off in a cell from a single zero.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
3) Quality control



Left: separating cells from empty droplets. Right: the plot every single-cell paper shows, or should.










Problem
What it looks like
What to do




Empty droplets
Low UMI barcodes below the knee
EmptyDrops rather than a hard cutoff


Ambient RNA
Marker genes of abundant cell types appearing everywhere
SoupX, CellBender, or DecontX


Doublets
High UMI and high gene count; two incompatible marker sets
Scrublet, DoubletFinder; ~1% per 1,000 cells loaded in droplet systems


Dying cells
High mitochondrial fraction, low gene count
Threshold on mito % — but tissue-specifically









WarningQC thresholds are analysis decisions, not cleaning






A mito cutoff of 5% is common — and wrong for cardiomyocytes, which are genuinely mitochondria-rich
A minimum-gene threshold of 500 removes debris — and also small, low-RNA cells such as platelets and some granulocytes

→ Every QC threshold removes a cell population. Look at what you are excluding before you exclude it, and report the thresholds.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
1) The standard pipeline
normalise  →  select highly variable genes  →  PCA
           →  build a k-nearest-neighbour graph
           →  cluster (Leiden)  →  UMAP for visualisation
           →  annotate clusters
⚠️ Note the order — UMAP is computed for display only. Clustering happens on the PCA/graph, not on the two-dimensional embedding.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
section: 2) ⚠️ How to read a UMAP responsibly
text:
2) ⚠️ How to read a UMAP responsibly
UMAP = a non-linear projection of tens of dimensions into two. Preserves local neighbourhoods reasonably; global structure badly.






WarningWhat a UMAP does not tell you






Distances between clusters are not meaningful — two clusters far apart are not necessarily more different than two that are close
Cluster sizes are not meaningful — area reflects the embedding, not cell number
Apparent connections are not trajectories — a thin bridge may be doublets, ambient RNA, or a parameter artifact
The layout changes with parameters and random seed — n_neighbors and min_dist visibly reshape it

→ A UMAP is a picture of your data, not a measurement of it. Any claim that matters should be supported by a number computed in the high-dimensional space.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
3) Clustering resolution is arbitrary



Same cells, same algorithm, one parameter changed.


Leiden clustering takes a resolution parameter.

Raise it → more clusters. Lower it → fewer
⚠️ No correct value, and no statistical criterion that settles it. The algorithm will happily split any cluster you ask it to

💡 What to do instead of agonising:

Check clusters against marker genes and known biology, not against a score
Check stability — does the cluster survive a different resolution, a different seed, a subsampled dataset?
Ask whether a “new” cluster at higher resolution has genuinely distinct markers, or just gradations of the same ones
✅ Report the resolution you used







WarningA cluster is not a cell type





Clusters can equally reflect:

cell state (activated vs. resting)
cell cycle phase
stress response
ambient contamination
donor identity

→ Naming a cluster after its top marker gene and treating it as a cell type is how the literature accumulates cell types that do not exist.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
4) Annotation

Marker-based — check known markers per cluster. ✅ Transparent. ⚠️ Circular: you find the cell types you looked for
Reference-based — map onto an annotated atlas (Azimuth, SingleR, scANVI). ✅ Fast and consistent. ⚠️ Inherits the reference’s vocabulary; cannot name anything the reference lacks

💡 Use both. Disagreements between them are informative.
🗺️ Reference-based annotation is the single-cell form of reference bias (🔗 W1 §2.3③) — a cell type absent from the atlas becomes invisible, or is mislabelled as its nearest neighbour.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
1) ⚠️ Why per-cell tests are wrong



The most consequential statistical error in the single-cell literature.








ImportantCells from one donor are not independent samples





A Wilcoxon or t-test across 5,400 cells from 6 donors treats those cells as 5,400 independent observations.
They are not. Cells from the same person share that person’s genetics, environment, medication, batch, and processing.
The consequence:

p-values inflated by many orders of magnitude
add cells → the p-value shrinks indefinitely
→ you are measuring how many cells you loaded, not how many people you studied

⚠️ Seurat’s default FindMarkers behaves this way.

✅ Appropriate for identifying cluster markers within one dataset — a descriptive task
❌ Not appropriate for comparing conditions

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
2) Pseudobulk
The fix — for each donor × cell type, sum the counts across cells.
→ a small matrix of pseudo-samples → analyse with DESeq2 or edgeR exactly as in 🔗 W4 §5.

Benchmarks consistently find pseudobulk controls false positives far better than per-cell tests
Mixed models with a donor random effect are a reasonable alternative — more power retained, more computation







TipThe design consequence





If the unit of replication is the donor → the number of donors is your n.
Three patients vs. three controls = n = 3, whether you sequenced 3,000 cells or 300,000.
→ This changes what a single-cell experiment should cost. Many published studies profile enormous numbers of cells from two or three individuals:

✅ excellent for describing what cell types exist
❌ uninformative for claiming a difference between conditions

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
3) Differential abundance
Often the interesting result is not that a cell type changed its expression, but that there is more or less of it.
⚠️ Proportions are compositional — one cell type expands → all others’ proportions fall by arithmetic. (The same problem as 🔗 W4 §4.2, and in a different guise 🔗 W7 §6.)

✅ Methods that handle it: scCODA, miloR, propeller, Dirichlet-multinomial models
❌ A χ² test on cell counts is not valid

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
1) Trajectory inference
Cells caught mid-differentiation can be ordered along a pseudotime axis by transcriptional similarity.

Tools: Monocle3, Slingshot, PAGA
RNA velocity (scVelo) adds direction by comparing unspliced to spliced reads

⚠️ Three caveats worth stating plainly:

A trajectory algorithm returns a trajectory for any dataset, including one with no underlying process
Pseudotime is not time — it measures neither rate nor duration
RNA velocity’s assumptions about splicing kinetics are contested, and known to fail for some genes and systems

→ Treat these as hypothesis generators. Lineage tracing or time-course sampling is what tests them.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
2) Cell–cell communication
CellPhoneDB, CellChat, NicheNet score ligand–receptor pairs between cluster pairs based on co-expression.
⚠️ Co-expression of a ligand and a receptor in two cell types is not evidence that they interact:

the cells may never be adjacent
the ligand may not be secreted
the protein may not be made at all (🔗 W6)

→ These predictions need spatial or functional validation.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
3) Spatial transcriptomics — the next step
Dissociation discards everything about where a cell was. Spatial methods keep it.

Spot-based (Visium) — captures transcripts on a grid. ✅ Whole transcriptome. ⚠️ Each spot may contain several cells
Imaging-based (MERFISH, Xenium, CosMx) — single-molecule imaging at subcellular resolution. ⚠️ A targeted gene panel, not the whole transcriptome

→ The same trade-off shape as everything else in this chapter: resolution vs. breadth.

title: W5. Single-cell Transcriptomics
text:
4) Reference atlases



Resource
What it gives you




Human Cell Atlas
Coordinated single-cell reference across human tissues


CELLxGENE
Browse, subset, and download hundreds of published datasets interactively


Tabula Sapiens
Multi-organ atlas from the same donors


Azimuth
Reference-based annotation, in the browser



💡 Before generating single-cell data, check whether the atlas already answers your question. For “which cell types express my gene”, it usually does.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Explain why mRNA is not a proxy for protein, and name the mechanisms responsible
Describe the bottom-up MS workflow and read an annotated MS2 spectrum
Choose between DDA, DIA, and targeted acquisition for a given question
⚠️ Explain the protein inference problem and what a “protein group” means
Distinguish LFQ, TMT, and SILAC, and explain TMT ratio compression
⚠️ Explain why proteomics data has missing values and why naive imputation is dangerous
Say when to use mass spectrometry and when to use an affinity platform

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
1) The correlation problem



Across genes, mRNA abundance explains roughly a fifth of the variance in protein abundance.



Proteins do the work — drug targets, biomarkers, enzymes
RNA-seq measures none of them directly

r ≈ 0.4 — read it carefully:

An across-genes correlation: gene A’s mRNA vs. gene A’s protein, over thousands of genes
Within one gene, across conditions → often better
⚠️ For the common question “gene X’s transcript went up — did the protein?” the honest answer from RNA-seq alone is probably, maybe

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
2) Where the other 80% goes

Translation efficiency — varies more than a hundred-fold between transcripts
Protein half-life — minutes to days. A stable protein accumulates from a modest transcript
Post-translational modification — changes activity with no change in abundance at all
Localisation — the same quantity of protein in the nucleus vs. cytoplasm is different biology
Complex stoichiometry — unassembled subunits are degraded → abundance set by the limiting partner







ImportantThe practical rule





Whenever a conclusion is about protein — a drug target, a biomarker, a signalling event —
mRNA evidence is a hypothesis, not a result.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
1) The bottom-up workflow



The workflow, and the spectrum at its heart.


Intact proteins are too large and heterogeneous to measure well → bottom-up proteomics digests them (almost always with trypsin, which cuts after lysine and arginine) and measures the peptides.

Digest the protein mixture into peptides
Separate by liquid chromatography over 30–120 minutes
MS1 survey scan — measure the m/z of everything eluting at this moment
Fragment selected peptides by collision (HCD/CID)
MS2 spectrum — measure the fragment masses
Database search — match the spectrum to a peptide sequence
Infer which proteins those peptides came from







WarningYou never observe a protein





Every step from ④ onwards is inference.

You observe peptide fragment masses
The protein identity is a conclusion drawn from them
→ §3.2 explains why that conclusion is sometimes ambiguous

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
2) Reading an MS2 spectrum
Fragmentation breaks the peptide backbone at different positions → a ladder.

b ions — retain the N-terminus
y ions — retain the C-terminus
The mass difference between consecutive ions in a series = one amino acid → this is how the sequence is read

💡 In practice a search engine does this by generating theoretical spectra for every peptide in a database and scoring the match, rather than reading sequences de novo.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
3) Acquisition strategies



Left: how the instrument decides what to fragment. Right: the downstream consequence you will actually feel.












DDA
DIA
Targeted (PRM/MRM)




What is fragmented
Top-N most intense precursors
Everything, in fixed m/z windows
A predefined list only


Proteins per run

Missing values across runs
⚠️ High
Low

Spectra

Quantitative precision

Best for

Validating a specific panel



DDA’s weakness — the selection is stochastic:

a low-abundance peptide picked in run 1 may be skipped in run 2, simply because something else was momentarily more intense
→ across 100 clinical samples, a matrix full of holes (§4)

DIA’s fix — fragment everything. Cost: far more complex spectra.

DIA-NN and Spectronaut — increasingly using machine-learning-predicted spectral libraries rather than experimental ones
→ what made DIA practical, and now the default for large cohort studies

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
1) Target–decoy FDR
The question — how do you know a peptide–spectrum match is real?
The trick:

Search the same spectra against a decoy database of reversed or shuffled sequences
Any decoy match is by definition false
→ the rate of decoy hits above a score threshold estimates the FDR among target hits

Convention: 1% FDR.
⚠️ 1% FDR at the peptide level does not give 1% FDR at the protein level — protein-level error accumulates, and single-peptide identifications are the least reliable.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
2) ⚠️ The protein inference problem



Peptides do not map cleanly onto proteins.








WarningShared peptides and protein groups





The problem:

Trypsin cuts proteins into peptides
Many peptides are shared between related proteins — paralogues, isoforms, family members
→ detect only a shared peptide, and several proteins are equally consistent with the data

How software resolves it — reports a protein group: a set of indistinguishable proteins with one representative accession.
⚠️ That representative is often the only name that reaches your results table, your figure, and your abstract.
What to check on any protein of interest:

How many unique (protein-specific) peptides support it? One is weak; two is a common minimum
Is it reported as part of a group? If so, which members?
Would the biological story change if a different group member were the real one?

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
3) Quantification strategies



Left: when the samples are combined determines how much technical variation they share. Right: the artifact specific to TMT.












LFQ
TMT / iTRAQ
SILAC




How

Isobaric chemical tags, one run
Heavy amino acids fed to cells


Samples per run
1

2–3

Never
After digestion
In culture


Applicable to
Anything, including tissue and plasma
Anything
Cultured cells only


Main weakness
Run-to-run drift, more missing values
⚠️ Ratio compression, batch structure
Not usable in humans




⚠️ Ratio compression
The mechanism:

In TMT, all samples are measured in one MS2 spectrum via reporter ions
The instrument’s isolation window is not perfectly selective
→ co-eluting background peptides get co-isolated and contribute their own reporter ions
→ the background is roughly equal across channels → it pulls every ratio toward 1

The magnitude — a genuine 8-fold change can be reported as 3-fold.
The fix — SPS-MS3 acquisition largely corrects it, at the cost of speed and sensitivity.


⚠️ TMT batch structure

An 18-plex TMT experiment analysing 90 samples requires 5 batches
Cases and controls unevenly distributed across batches → 🔗 W1 §4.3’s confounding problem, reproduced exactly

→ Randomise, and include a common reference channel in every batch so batches can be aligned.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
1) Two kinds of missing

MNAR — missing not at random. The protein was below the limit of detection. The missingness is informative: it tells you the abundance was low
MAR / MCAR — missing at random. DDA happened not to select it, or the peptide had a poor retention time that run. Uninformative

⚠️ Real data is a mixture, and the proportion depends heavily on abundance — exactly what the left panel shows.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
2) ⚠️ Why imputation is dangerous






WarningThe commonest way to manufacture a proteomics false positive





The recipe:

Replace missing values with a small constant, or the minimum observed value
→ a protein detected in all controls and none of the cases now has a large, extremely significant fold change
→ for every protein sitting near the detection limit

The signature — a volcano plot with a suspicious cloud of “highly significant” hits, all at large fold changes, all driven by imputed values rather than measurements.
Better practice:

✅ Filter first — require detection in, say, ≥70% of samples in at least one group before testing
✅ Match the method to the mechanism — MNAR needs left-censored imputation (QRILC, MinProb); MAR needs something like kNN. Perseus’s “replace missing from normal distribution” is a MNAR method and should not be applied indiscriminately
✅ Or do not impute — MSstats and limma handle missingness in the model rather than filling it in
✅ Always report how much was missing, how you filtered, what you imputed — then check whether your top hits survive without imputation

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
1) The dynamic range problem



Plasma spans more than ten orders of magnitude. No single method covers it.


Plasma — the most clinically desirable sample, and the hardest to analyse.

Albumin and immunoglobulins alone ≈ half the protein mass
The top 20 proteins ≈ 99% of it
The biomarkers you want — cytokines, tissue leakage proteins, tumour-derived proteins — sit ten orders of magnitude below

→ Unfractionated MS covers perhaps five to six orders.
→ Hence depletion of abundant proteins, extensive fractionation, or enrichment — all of which add variability and cost.

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
2) Affinity platforms
Two technologies dominate large-cohort plasma proteomics. Neither uses mass spectrometry.

Olink (PEA) — a pair of antibodies binds the target; when both bind, attached DNA oligos hybridise, are amplified, and read out by sequencing or qPCR. Requiring two binding events gives high specificity
SomaScan — modified DNA aptamers (SOMAmers) bind targets; abundance read from aptamer quantity on an array










Mass spectrometry
Affinity (Olink / SomaScan)




Targets
Unbiased — whatever is there
Predefined panel only


Proteins measured
~3,000 (plasma, with effort)
Thousands, up to ~11,000


Sensitivity
Limited by dynamic range
Reaches pg/mL


Sample volume
µL–mL
A few µL


Throughput
Moderate
Very high — biobank scale


What is measured
Peptide sequence
Binding to a reagent


Isoforms and PTMs
Detectable
Generally not distinguished









WarningAffinity assays measure binding, not identity





An Olink or SomaScan readout is a binding signal — and binding can be affected by things other than concentration:

Cross-reactivity — the reagent binds something else
Epitope-altering variants — a missense variant in the epitope reduces binding → appears as reduced protein level

⚠️ In pQTL studies this produces spurious cis-signals. A known confounder requiring explicit checking

Platform disagreement — Olink and SomaScan measurements of the same protein correlate only moderately for many targets. Which one is “right” is often unresolved

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
3) 💊 Proteogenomics and pQTLs
pQTL — a genetic variant associated with a protein’s abundance. The protein analogue of an eQTL (🔗 W2 §4.4, 🔗 W4 §7.4).
Population-scale plasma proteomics on tens of thousands of biobank participants has made these available at scale.
This closes a loop that runs through the whole course:
GWAS hit (W2)        → points to a locus
pQTL (W6)            → which protein's level that locus controls
Colocalization       → do the two signals share a causal variant?
Mendelian rand. (W2) → does that protein causally affect disease?
        ↓
a genetically validated, druggable target (🔗 W2 §6.3)
⚠️ Distinguish:

cis-pQTL — variant near the protein’s own gene. Strong evidence, but check for epitope effects
trans-pQTL — variant elsewhere. Biologically interesting (a regulator, a clearance mechanism), harder to interpret

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
1) Post-translational modifications
Phosphoproteomics — the main clinical example. Signalling is regulated by phosphorylation, and total protein abundance says nothing about it.
The workflow adds an enrichment step (TiO₂, IMAC), because phosphopeptides are a small fraction of the total.
Two analysis-specific issues:

⚠️ Site localisation — a peptide may contain several possible sites, and the spectrum may not distinguish them. Search engines report a localisation probability → treat sites below ~0.75 as uncertain
⚠️ Normalisation to total protein — a phosphopeptide can rise simply because the protein rose. Interpreting phosphorylation as signalling requires knowing the protein level too

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
2) Structure in the AlphaFold era
Accurate structure prediction has changed what a protein list can support — variant effect interpretation, docking, cross-linking MS interpretation.
⚠️ A prediction is a model:

confidence scores (pLDDT) matter
disordered regions are predicted poorly
a predicted structure is not evidence of a conformation in vivo

title: W6. Proteomics
text:
3) ⚠️ Common pitfalls

Keratin contamination — skin and hair keratins are the classic proteomics contaminant. Keratins in your top hits → the problem is at the bench
Dynamic range — failing to deplete or fractionate plasma means you measured albumin
Digestion efficiency — incomplete tryptic digestion varies between samples. A real source of quantitative noise
Storage and freeze–thaw — plasma proteomes are sensitive to pre-analytical handling: collection tube, time to freezing, freeze–thaw cycles. ⚠️ In biobank studies this is a systematic confounder if collection protocols differed between groups

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Explain why microbiome study design is dominated by confounders and contamination
Choose between 16S amplicon and shotgun sequencing for a given question
Distinguish alpha from beta diversity and interpret a PCoA with PERMANOVA
⚠️ Explain why compositional data breaks standard statistics, and what CLR does about it
⚠️ Explain why differential abundance methods disagree, and how to report results honestly
Judge whether a microbiome–disease association is cause, consequence, or artifact
Read any omics paper critically — the closing skill of the course

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
1) What lives where

The human body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — the once-quoted 10:1 ratio was an overestimate; current best estimate ≈ 1:1
Almost all of them are in the colon




Left: body sites are effectively different ecosystems. Right: and healthy individuals differ enormously from one another.


Two facts from this figure shape every microbiome study:

Body sites are not comparable — gut, oral, skin, vaginal, and airway communities differ from each other more than most disease states differ from health
⚠️ Between-person variation is enormous — two healthy adults can share a minority of their gut species

→ detecting a disease effect requires large samples
→ and most published microbiome studies are small

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
2) Disease associations, honestly
Microbiome differences have been reported for nearly every disease studied. The strength of evidence varies enormously — be explicit about the tier:







Evidence level
Examples




Causal, mechanistically established
C. difficile infection (and FMT as treatment); H. pylori and gastric cancer


Strong, with animal-model support
Diet–microbiome–metabolite axes; bile acid metabolism; some drug metabolism (e.g. digoxin, irinotecan)


Reproducible association, causality unclear
IBD, colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, obesity


Widely reported, poorly replicated
Most neuropsychiatric and behavioural “gut–brain” associations



💡 Reading a microbiome paper → place it on this ladder before evaluating anything else.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
1) Pre-analytical variation
Microbiome measurements are unusually sensitive to what happened before sequencing:

Collection and storage — time at room temperature changes composition; freeze–thaw cycles matter; preservative buffers differ in their effects
⚠️ DNA extraction — the single largest technical source of variation

Gram-positive bacteria have tough cell walls
→ bead-beating protocols recover them; gentle protocols do not
→ two labs using different kits report different communities from the same stool

Primer choice (§3.1①) and sequencing platform

The practical consequence:

✅ comparisons within a study — reasonable
⚠️ comparisons between studies — treacherous. Meta-analyses must model study as a batch variable

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
2) ⚠️ Confounders

Diet — the dominant environmental determinant of gut composition, and almost never measured adequately
Medications — proton pump inhibitors, metformin, antibiotics, and laxatives all have large, well-documented microbiome effects







WarningThe metformin lesson






Early studies → a distinctive gut microbiome signature in type 2 diabetes
Much of that signature turned out to be an effect of metformin, not of diabetes
Treatment-naive patients analysed separately → the picture changed substantially

Ask of any case–control microbiome study: were the cases on different drugs?
Almost always they were.



Also collect and adjust for: age · sex · BMI · bowel movement frequency and stool consistency (Bristol scale — a surprisingly strong covariate) · transit time · geography.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
3) ⚠️ The kit-ome



Contaminant fraction is a function of how much real biomass you started with.


The mechanism — extraction kits and PCR reagents contain bacterial DNA.

Stool → negligible
Blood, tissue biopsy, placenta → the sample may contain fewer bacterial cells than the kit does
→ most of what you sequence came out of the kit

⚠️ Several high-profile low-biomass findings — including a healthy placental microbiome and some tumour-microbiome results — were subsequently attributed largely to contamination.






ImportantWhat a credible low-biomass study does






✅ Sequences extraction blanks and no-template controls in every batch
✅ Uses them — decontam and similar tools identify contaminants by (i) prevalence in blanks and (ii) inverse correlation with DNA concentration
✅ Records DNA concentration as a covariate
✅ Reports results with and without decontamination

⚠️ A low-biomass paper that does not mention negative controls → that is the first thing to note.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
1) 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing
The logic — the 16S rRNA gene is present in all bacteria and archaea, and alternates:

conserved regions — where universal primers bind
variable regions — which differ between taxa

→ amplify one or two variable regions, sequence, classify.

① ⚠️ Primer and copy-number bias

Different variable regions (V3–V4, V4, V1–V2) give different answers → studies using different regions are not directly comparable
“Universal” primers are not universal — some taxa are amplified poorly or not at all
16S copy number varies from 1 to ~15 per genome → read proportions are not cell proportions



② OTUs vs. ASVs

OTU — reads clustered at 97% similarity. The threshold was chosen to absorb sequencing error
ASV — amplicon sequence variant (DADA2, Deblur). Models the error process and resolves exact sequences

ASVs are now standard, with one large practical advantage: comparable across studies, because an ASV is a sequence rather than a cluster defined by one dataset.


③ Resolution limit

16S generally reaches genus level
Species-level assignment → unreliable
Strain-level → impossible

⚠️ Papers reporting species-level 16S results are over-claiming — and the difference matters: E. coli strains range from commensal to lethal.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
2) Shotgun metagenomics
Sequence all DNA in the sample.

Taxonomic profiling at species and often strain level (MetaPhlAn, Kraken2/Bracken, StrainPhlAn)
Functional profiling — which genes and pathways are present (HUMAnN)

💡 The crucial addition: distantly related organisms often carry the same functional capacity → function may matter more than identity

Non-bacterial members — viruses, fungi, plasmids
Assembly into MAGs — recovering genomes of uncultured organisms

The costs:

⚠️ ~an order of magnitude more expensive
⚠️ needs high microbial biomass and low host DNA — a tissue biopsy may be >99% human reads
⚠️ much heavier computation

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
3) ✅ Choosing



Your question
Use




Broad survey, hundreds of samples, limited budget
16S

16S


Species or strain resolution
Shotgun


What the community does, not just who is there
Shotgun


Viruses, fungi, or mobile elements
Shotgun

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
1) Alpha diversity — within a sample

Richness — how many taxa. ⚠️ Strongly dependent on sequencing depth
Shannon, Simpson — combine richness and evenness. Two samples with identical richness can have very different Shannon values
Faith’s PD — richness weighted by phylogenetic distance

💡 Report at least one richness-type and one evenness-type index. They can disagree, and the disagreement is informative.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
2) ⚠️ The rarefaction debate
The problem — sequencing depth varies between samples, and richness rises with depth. Something must be done.
Rarefaction (subsample all to equal depth)
   → was standard
   → criticised as statistically wasteful ("waste not, want not") — it discards data
   → model-based normalisation proposed instead
   → more recent work argues rarefaction is robust in practice
                                        for diversity and ordination
   → the debate is not settled
✅ The defensible position — do something explicit, say what you did, and check whether the conclusion survives the alternative.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
3) Beta diversity — between samples

Bray–Curtis — abundance-weighted dissimilarity. The default
Jaccard — presence/absence only
UniFrac (weighted / unweighted) — incorporates phylogenetic relatedness

Visualised by PCoA, tested with PERMANOVA.






WarningReport R², not only p






PERMANOVA on a few hundred samples will detect almost anything
p tells you the groups differ
R² tells you how much of the variation the grouping explains — in microbiome studies typically 1–8%

→ “Significantly different community composition (p = 0.001)” with R² = 0.02 means the disease explains 2% of the variation, and 98% is something else.
Both numbers belong in the abstract.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
1) The problem



Only one taxon changed. Three others appear to have decreased.


Sequencing measures proportions. The total is fixed by how many reads you bought, not by how many bacteria were in the sample.

→ one taxon expands
→ every other taxon’s proportion falls, by arithmetic
→ with no biological change at all

🔗 You have now met this three times:

RNA-seq composition effects (W4 §4.2)
single-cell differential abundance (W5 §6.3)
here

⚠️ Microbiome data is the most extreme case — the changes are large and the taxa are few.






TipThe fix that actually solves it





Compositional problems arise because you only measured proportions.
Quantitative microbiome profiling recovers absolute abundances:

spike in a known standard, or
measure total microbial load by flow cytometry or qPCR

→ dissolves the problem entirely. Not yet routine — and it should be more so.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
2) The CLR transformation
Without absolute measurements, work with ratios rather than proportions.
CLR (centred log-ratio) — divide each taxon by the geometric mean of all taxa in that sample, take the log.

✅ Ratios between taxa within a sample are unaffected by the total → CLR-based analyses are not distorted by the fixed sum
⚠️ Undefined for zeros → a pseudocount must be added, and microbiome matrices are extremely sparse

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
3) ⚠️ Differential abundance methods disagree



Eight methods, one dataset. The disagreement is not marginal.








WarningA well-documented, unresolved problem





A large benchmark across dozens of real datasets found:

methods produce substantially different results on the same data
some widely used methods — LEfSe and edgeR among them — call far more taxa than others
→ poor agreement overall

Why they differ — normalisation, whether compositionality is modelled, zero handling, and how conservative they are:







Method
Approach




ALDEx2
CLR + Monte Carlo sampling from the Dirichlet posterior. Conservative


ANCOM-BC
Estimates and corrects a sampling-fraction bias per sample


LinDA
Linear model on CLR data with bias correction. Fast, handles complex designs


MaAsLin2
Flexible general linear models, multiple normalisation options


DESeq2 / edgeR
Borrowed from RNA-seq. ⚠️ Their normalisations assume most features are unchanged — often false here


LEfSe
Widely used. ⚠️ Known to be liberal



How to report honestly:

✅ Run at least two methods with different assumptions
✅ Report the intersection as the confident set, the union as exploratory
✅ Treat a taxon called by only one method as unconfirmed
✅ State which method produced the headline result — and show it is not the only one that would have




🔗 The same lesson as W4 §5.3 — if your conclusion depends on which tool you ran, you do not yet have a conclusion. Simply far more acute here.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
1) Artifact

Different extraction batch
Different collection protocol
Different sequencing run
Contamination
Unequal depth

→ §2 covers this, and it should be excluded first.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
2) Confounding
Diet · medication · BMI · transit time · age · geography.
→ Cases differ from controls in many ways besides disease, and the microbiome responds to most of them.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
3) Reverse causation
Disease changes the gut environment:

inflammation → altered oxygen tension → favours facultative anaerobes such as Enterobacteriaceae
diarrhoea → shortened transit time
reduced appetite → changed substrate availability

⚠️ A disease-associated microbiome is at least as likely to be a consequence as a cause — and cross-sectional designs cannot distinguish them.

title: W7. Metagenomics
text:
4) Causation
What would actually establish it:

Longitudinal sampling — does the microbiome change before disease onset?
Gnotobiotic transfer — does colonising a germ-free mouse with patient microbiota transfer the phenotype? Strong evidence, ⚠️ with the caveat that mouse and human gut environments differ substantially
Intervention — FMT, defined consortia, targeted antibiotics

✅ FMT for recurrent C. difficile — the clear success
⚠️ Other indications — far more mixed

Mendelian randomization — human genetic variants associated with microbial abundance as instruments. ⚠️ Attractive in principle, but host genetic effects on the microbiome are weak → few and weak instruments (🔗 W2 §6.2)







ImportantThe honest default





For most microbiome–disease associations in the current literature, the direction of causality is unknown.
→ A paper that describes an association and then discusses mechanism as though causality were established is doing something you should notice.
